<!-- stabtheorem-1: body_md -->
For every family $\mathbf W$ displayed in the table below, 
\[ 
\mathrm{G}_p(\mathbf{W}_\infty; t)=\mathrm{P}_p(\mathbf{W},t)\;\mathrm{G}_p(\mathbf{B}_\infty; t) 
- 
\begin{cases} 
0&\text{if $p\neq 2$},\\ 
\mathrm{R}(\mathbf{W},t)&\text{if $p=2$}, 
\end{cases} 
\] 
where $\mathrm{P}_p(\mathbf{W},t)$ and $\mathrm{R}(\mathbf{W},t)$ are the 
rational functions from the following table: 
\begin{center} 
\renewcommand{1.2}{2} 
\begin{tabular}{|c||c|c|c|c|c|} \hline 
$\mathrm{P}\backslash\mathbf{W}$ & $\mathbf{C}_\infty$ & $\mathbf{D}_\infty$ &  
$\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_\infty$ & $\widetilde{\mathbf{C}}_\infty$ & $\widetilde{\mathbf{D}}_\infty$ \\ \hline\hline 
$\mathrm{P}_{p\neq 2}(\mathbf{W},t)$ & $\frac{1}{1-t}$ & $1$ & $\frac{1}{1-t}$ & $\frac{1}{(1-t)^2}$ & $1$ \\ \hline  
$\mathrm{P}_2(\mathbf{W},t)$ & $\frac{1}{1-t}$ & $\frac{t^2}{1-t}+1$ & $\frac{t^2}{(1-t)^2}+1$ 
& $\frac{1}{(1-t)^2}$ & $\left(\frac{1-t+t^2}{1-t}\right)^2$ \\ \hline  
$\mathrm{R}(\mathbf{W},t)$ & $0$ & $\frac{t^2}{1-t}$ & $\frac{t^2}{(1-t)^2}$ 
& $0$ & $\left(\frac{1-t+t^2}{1-t}\right)^2-1$ \\ \hline  
\end{tabular} 
\end{center}
<!-- end stabtheorem-1 -->
<!-- defnr-1: body_md -->
The \textit{Artin group} $\mathbb{A}(W)$ associated with a Coxeter system $(W,S)$ 
is the group generated by symbols $\sigma_s$, where $s\in S$, subject to the relations 
\[ 
\Pi\left(\sigma_s,\sigma_{s^\prime}:m_{s,s^\prime}\right)= 
\Pi\left(\sigma_{s^\prime},\sigma_s:m_{s,s^\prime}\right),\; 
\text{where $s,s^\prime\in S,\;s\neq s^\prime,\;m_{s,s^\prime}\neq\infty$}. 
\] 
We say that the Artin group $\mathbb{A}(W)$ is \emph{spherical} 
or \emph{affine} when the corresponding Coxeter group 
$W$ is spherical or affine, respectively.
<!-- end defnr-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
For the Coxeter group $W$, let 
\[ 
\mathbf{X}(W):=\Big((I_W\times I_W)\smallsetminus 
\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal{H}(W)}(H\times H)\Big)\Big{/}W, 
\] 
where the action of $W$ on $I_W\times I_W$ is diagonal. 
Then $\pi_1\bigl(\mathbf X(W)\bigr)\cong\mathbb A(W)$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- hyp-1: body_md -->
\label{Hyp_A} 
For any Coxeter group $W$, 
the space $\mathbf{X}(W)$ is homotopically equivalent to 
the Eilenberg--MacLane space $K(\mathbb A(W),1)$.
<!-- end hyp-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{Sal} 
Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system. 
Then the graded group $H^*(\mathbf{X}(W);\mathbb{Z})$ 
is isomorphic to the cohomology of the cochain 
complex $\mathbf{S}(W)$ defined for $q\geqslant 0$ as follows: 
\[ 
\mathbf{S}^q(W)= 
\bigoplus_{P\subset S,\; |P|=q,\; |W_P|<\infty} 
\mathbb Z\cdot P . 
\] 
After fixing a linear order on $S$, the differential of the complex $\mathbf{S}(W)$ is given by 
\[ 
\partial_W(P)= 
\sum_{s\in S\setminus P,\; |W_{P\cup\{s\}}|<\infty} 
(-1)^{\epsilon(s,P)} 
\left.\frac{W_{P\cup\{s\}}(t)}{W_P(t)}\right|_{t=-1} 
\,(P\cup\{s\}), 
\] 
where 
\[ 
\epsilon(s,P)= 
\bigl|\{\,t\in P\mid t<s\,\}\bigr|, 
\] 
and $W_P(t)$ denotes the Poincaré polynomial of the finite Coxeter group $W_P$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- defnr-2: body_md -->
\label{DefSal} 
The complex $\mathbf S(W)$, defined in Theorem~\ref{Sal}, 
is called the algebraic \textit{Salvetti complex} of the Coxeter group 
$W$.
<!-- end defnr-2 -->
<!-- defnr-3: body_md -->
\label{ElGr} 
An abelian group is called \emph{squarefree-torsion} if it has no 
elements of order $p^2$ for any prime $p$.
<!-- end defnr-3 -->
<!-- defnr-4: body_md -->
\label{DotPlus} 
Let $M$ be a free module with a chosen basis $B$, and let 
$\tau:M\to M$ be an involution preserving $B$. If 
$u=\sum_{b\in B}\lambda_b b$, 
we write 
\[ 
u\mathbf{\dotplus}\tau(u) 
\] 
for the element obtained from $u+\tau(u)$ by counting each 
$\tau$-fixed basis element only once.
<!-- end defnr-4 -->
<!-- defnr-5: body_md -->
\label{Ez} 
Denote by 
\[ 
\mathrm E[z]:=\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant0}\mathbb Z\cdot z^{(i)}, 
\qquad w(z^{(i)})=i 
\] 
the graded $\mathbb{Z}$--algebra with multiplication defined by 
$z^{(i)}\cdot z^{(j)}:=\pi(i,j)z^{(i+j)}$. 
 
In addition, define its graded subalgebra $\Gamma[z]:=\bigoplus_{i\geqslant 0}\mathbb{Z}\cdot z^{(2i)}$.
<!-- end defnr-5 -->
<!-- defnr-6: body_md -->
\textit{The braid group $\mathbf B_n$ on $n\geqslant1$ strands} 
is the Artin group $\mathbb A(A_{n-1})$, where $A_0$ denotes the 
trivial Coxeter group.
<!-- end defnr-6 -->
<!-- defnr-7: body_md -->
Let $\mathrm{A}:=\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{n\geqslant 0}\mathrm{A}(n)$ be the direct sum 
of complexes, where $\mathrm{A}(n)=\mathbf{S}(A_{n-1})$ for $n>0$, 
and $\mathrm{A}(0)$ is the complex $\mathbb{Z}$ concentrated in degree~$0$. 
We denote the differential of the complex $\mathrm{A}$ by $\partial$. 
We extend the notation by setting $\mathrm A(n)=0$ for $n<0$.
<!-- end defnr-7 -->
<!-- defnr-8: body_md -->
\label{comp} 
A \textit{composition} is a~sequence $\alpha=(n_1,\dots,n_l)$ 
of positive integers. 
The integers $n_i$ are called the \textit{parts} of~$\alpha$, 
the number $l(\alpha):=l$ is its \textit{length}, 
and the sum $n_1+\dots+n_l$ is its \textit{size}.
<!-- end defnr-8 -->
<!-- lmr-1: body_md -->
\label{Comp} 
{\rm(a)} For $n\geqslant 1$, there is a~canonical bijection 
\[ 
\varepsilon:\big\{P\subset\llbracket n-1\rrbracket\big\}\longrightarrow R(n) 
\quad\text{with}\quad\varepsilon(P)\in R_{n-|P|}(n). 
\] 
 
{\rm(b)} 
Let $n\geqslant 2,P\subset\llbracket n-1\rrbracket$, and let 
$s\in\llbracket n-1\rrbracket\setminus P$. 
If $\varepsilon(P)=(n_1,\dots,n_a)$, then 
there exists a unique $i\in\{1,\dots,a-1\}$ with 
\[ 
\varepsilon\bigl(P\cup\{s\}\bigr)=(n_1,\dots,n_{i-1},n_i+n_{i+1},n_{i+2},\dots,n_a). 
\]
<!-- end lmr-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
(a) Let $\llbracket n-1\rrbracket\setminus P=\{q_1<\dots<q_r\}$. 
Set $q_0=0$ and $q_{r+1}=n$. Define the map $\varepsilon$ by 
\[ 
\varepsilon(P):=(q_1-q_0,q_2-q_1,\dots,q_{r+1}-q_r)\in R_{n-|P|}(n). 
\] 
The inverse map $\varepsilon^{-1}$ on 
a composition $\alpha=(n_1,\dots,n_a)$ of size $n$ is given by 
\[ 
\varepsilon^{-1}(\alpha)=P_\alpha:=\llbracket n-1\rrbracket\setminus\{t_1,\dots,t_{a-1}\},\qquad 
t_i:=n_1+\dots+n_i\quad(i\in\llbracket a-1\rrbracket). 
\] 
The identities $\varepsilon(P_\alpha)=\alpha$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}(\varepsilon(P))=P$ 
show that $\varepsilon$ is a bijection. 
\smallskip 
 
(b) Since 
$\llbracket n-1\rrbracket\setminus P=\{t_1,\dots,t_{a-1}\}$, 
it follows that $s=t_i$ for a unique index $i$. 
Hence, claim (b) follows directly from the construction of $\varepsilon(P)$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lmr-2: body_md -->
\label{WA} 
Let $(W,\llbracket n-1\rrbracket)$ be the Coxeter system of type $A_{n-1}$, 
and let $P\subseteq\llbracket n-1\rrbracket$. 
Assume that $\varepsilon(P)=(n_1,\dots,n_a)$. 
Then, for any $s\in\llbracket n-1\rrbracket\setminus P$, 
let $i(s)$ be the unique index determined by 
Lemma~\ref{Comp}(b). We have 
\[ 
\left.\frac{W_{P\cup\{s\}}(t)}{W_P(t)}\right|_{t=-1}=\pi(n_{i(s)},n_{i(s)+1}). 
\]
<!-- end lmr-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\langle P\rangle=\langle P_1\rangle\times\dots\times\langle P_m\rangle$ 
be the decomposition of $\langle P\rangle\subseteq A_{n-1}$ 
into the direct product of its irreducible parabolic subgroups. 
By the construction of $\varepsilon$, the subgroups 
$\langle P_r\rangle$ for $1\le r\le m$ correspond bijectively 
to the parts $|P_r|+1$ of the composition $\varepsilon(P)$. 
The remaining parts of $\varepsilon(P)$ are equal to $1$. 
 
By the multiplicativity of Poincaré polynomials under direct products of Coxeter groups, 
the Poincaré polynomial $W_P(t)$, where $\varepsilon(P)=(n_1,\dots,n_a)$, satisfies 
\[ 
W_P(t)=A_{n_1-1}(t)\cdot{\dots}\cdot A_{n_a-1}(t). 
\] 
Then Lemma \ref{Comp}(b) and a routine calculation imply 
that for $s\in\llbracket n-1\rrbracket\setminus P$ and $i=i(s)$, we have 
\[ 
\left.\frac{W_{P\cup\{s\}}(t)}{W_P(t)}\right|_{t=-1}= 
\left.\frac{A_{n_i+n_{i+1}-1}(t)}{A_{n_i-1}(t)\cdot A_{n_{i+1}-1}(t)}\right|_{t=-1}=\pi(n_i,n_{i+1}). 
\qedhere 
\]
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{FuchsD} 
The complex $\mathrm{A}(n)$ is canonically isomorphic to the complex with basis 
\[ 
e(n_1,\dots,n_a):=(-1)^{\nu(n_1,\dots,n_a)}(n_1,\dots,n_a), 
\] 
where $(n_1,\dots,n_a)$ runs over all compositions of size~$n$, 
and with the differential given by 
\[ 
\partial\bigl(e(n_1,\dots,n_a)\bigr)= 
\sum_{i=1}^{a-1}(-1)^i\pi(n_i,n_{i+1})\cdot 
e(n_1,\dots,n_i+n_{i+1},\dots,n_a). 
\] 
Moreover, $\mathrm{A}^q(n)$ is the linear span of the elements $\{e(n_1,\dots,n_a)\mid n_1+\dots+n_a-a=q\}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since, by linearity, the map $\varepsilon$ canonically identifies $\mathrm{A}(n)$ 
with the $\mathbb{Z}$-module generated by the set of all compositions of size~$n$, 
the elements $e(n_1,\dots,n_a)$ form a basis of $\mathrm{A}(n)$. 
Combining the preceding discussion with Theorem~\ref{Sal}, 
we see that the differential $\partial$ acts on a composition 
$c=(n_1,\dots,n_a)$ of size $n$ by 
\[ 
\partial(c)=\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{a-1} 
(-1)^{\sum_{k=1}^i n_k-i}\,\pi(n_i,n_{i+1})\cdot c_i, 
\] 
where $c_i=(n_1,\dots,n_i+n_{i+1},\dots,n_a)$. 
 
In $\nu(c)$, the coefficient of $n_k$ is $a-k$. 
In $\nu(c_i)$, the composition length is $a-1$. 
Thus, for $k \leqslant i$, the coefficient of $n_k$ shifts down 
to $(a-1)-k$, while for $k > i+1$ it remains $a-k$ because 
its position index also shifts down by 1. 
Therefore, 
\[ 
\nu(c)-\nu(c_i)=\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^i n_k. 
\] 
Substituting $c_i=(-1)^{\nu(c_i)}e(c_i)$, the total exponent of 
$-1$ for the $i$-th term is 
\[ 
\nu(c)+\nu(c_i)+\sum_{k=1}^i n_k-i. 
\] 
Modulo 2, this exponent is congruent to: 
\[ 
\nu(c)-\nu(c_i)+\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^i n_k-i=2\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^i n_k-i\equiv i \pmod 2. 
\] 
This yields the asserted expression for 
$\partial\bigl(e(c)\bigr)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- defnr-9: body_md -->
The complex $\mathrm{A}(n)$ described in Theorem~\ref{FuchsD} 
is called the \emph{Fuchs complex} of degree~$n$. 
Its basis, consisting of the elements $e(n_1,\dots,n_a)$, is called the \emph{Fuchs basis}.
<!-- end defnr-9 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{SEF} 
Define a homomorphism of abelian groups 
\[ 
\Phi:\mathrm{A}:=\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{n\geqslant 0}\mathrm{A}(n) 
\longrightarrow C_*\bigl(\mathrm{E}[z]\bigr) 
\] 
by 
\[ 
\Phi(e(0))=z^{(0)},\qquad 
\Phi\bigl(e(n_1,\ldots,n_a)\bigr) 
= 
\bigl[z^{(n_1)}|\cdots|z^{(n_a)}\bigr]. 
\] 
Then, for each $n\geqslant 0$ and each $q$, the map $\Phi$ restricts to 
an isomorphism of abelian groups 
\[ 
\Phi_n^q:\mathrm{A}^q(n)\xrightarrow{\;\cong\;} 
C^{(n)}_{n-q}\bigl(\mathrm{E}[z]\bigr). 
\] 
Moreover, this isomorphism identifies the coboundary operator  
$\partial$ of the Fuchs complex with the differential $b$ 
in the normalized Hochschild complex $C_*(E[z];\mathbb Z)$: 
for every $x\in \mathrm{A}^q(n)$ one has 
\[ 
\Phi_n^{q+1}(\partial x)=b\,\Phi_n^q(x). 
\] 
Define $H^q(\mathbf{B}_0):=H^q(\mathrm{A}(0))$. 
Then, for $n\geqslant 0$, 
\[ 
H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong 
H^{(n)}_{n-q}\bigl(\mathrm{E}[z]\bigr). 
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The map $\Phi$ is clearly a bijection on the basis elements of weight 
$n$, and it sends $\mathrm{A}^q(n)$ onto 
$C^{(n)}_{n-q}(\mathrm{E}[z])$. It remains only to compare the 
differentials. By Theorem~\ref{FuchsD}, 
\[ 
\partial e(n_1,\ldots,n_a) 
=\sum_{i=1}^{a-1}(-1)^i\pi(n_i,n_{i+1})\, 
e(n_1,\ldots,n_i+n_{i+1},\ldots,n_a). 
\] 
On the other hand, the Hochschild differential on $C_*(\mathrm{E}[z])$ 
gives 
\[ 
b\bigl[z^{(n_1)}|\cdots|z^{(n_a)}\bigr] 
= 
\sum_{i=1}^{a-1} 
(-1)^i 
\bigl[z^{(n_1)}|\cdots|z^{(n_i)}z^{(n_{i+1})}|\cdots|z^{(n_a)}\bigr]. 
\] 
Since 
$z^{(n_i)}z^{(n_{i+1})}=\pi(n_i,n_{i+1})\,z^{(n_i+n_{i+1})}$, 
we obtain $\Phi_n^{q+1}(\partial x)=b\,\Phi_n^q(x)$ 
for every $x\in\mathrm{A}^q(n)$. Hence $\Phi$ induces the stated 
isomorphism in cohomology.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remnr-1: body_md -->
\label{rmFuchs} 
Fuchs introduced the complex $\mathrm{A}(n)\otimes\mathbb{F}_2$ in \cite{Fuchs} 
and used it to compute $H^q(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{F}_2)$, 
long before the Salvetti complex became known. 
In contrast to the algebraic approach adopted in this section, 
Fuchs defined the elements $e(m_1,\dots,m_a)$ geometrically, as a  
cellular decomposition of the one-point compactification of the space of monic polynomials 
\[ 
t^n+a_{n-1}t^{n-1}+\dots+a_0\in\mathbb C[t] 
\] 
without multiple roots. The latter space, before compactification, 
is well known to be an open manifold that serves as a classifying 
space for the braid group $\mathbf B_n$. 
Fuchs extracted the cohomology of the group from the cellular cohomology  
of this compactification by invoking Alexander duality (see~\cite{Fuchs}). 
Later, Fuchs computed the action of the coboundary operator on his cellular decomposition 
over the integers, though this result remained unpublished. 
It served as the starting point for my note \cite{FW}.
<!-- end remnr-1 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{HGIso} 
There is a canonical isomorphism 
\begin{equation}\label{HAn1} 
H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{\left\lceil\frac{q}{2}\right\rceil\leqslant r\leqslant\min\left\{q-1,\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}} 
H_{2r-q}^{(2r)}\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)&\text{if $q\geqslant 2$ and $n\geqslant 2$},\\ 
\mathbb{Z}&\text{if $q\in\{0,1\}$ and $n\geqslant 2$},\\ 
\mathbb{Z}&\text{if $q=0$ and $n\in\{0,1\}$},\\ 
0&\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The cases $n=0,1$ follow directly from the definitions. 
For $n\geqslant2$, the cases $q=0,1$ follow from 
\eqref{HAn}. Suppose now that $n\geqslant2$ and $q\geqslant2$. 
 
It is clear that $C_{2r-q}^{(2r)}\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)={0}$ for $r>q$. 
If $r=q$, then 
$C_q^{(2q)}\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)=\mathbb{Z}\cdot [z^{(2)}|\dots|z^{(2)}]$, 
where $z^{(2)}$ is repeated $q$ times. 
Since $b\bigl([z^{(2)}|\dots|z^{(2)}]\bigr)\neq 0$, 
it follows that $H_q^{(2q)}\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)\cong 0$. 
Hence, $r\leqslant q-1$, and the required statement follows from 
isomorphism \eqref{HAn}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corr-1: body_md -->
\label{ArnRS} 
There are canonical isomorphisms: 
\begin{itemize} 
    \item[$\mathrm{(a)}$] $H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong H^q(\mathbf{B}_{n+1})$ if $n$ is even. 
    \item[$\mathrm{(b)}$] If $q\geqslant 2$ and $n\geqslant 2q-2$, then $H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong H^q(\mathbf{B}_{2q-2})$. 
    \item[$\mathrm{(c)}$] $H^2(\mathbf{B}_n)=0$. 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end corr-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Claims $\mathrm{(a)}$ and $\mathrm{(b)}$ follow directly from the isomorphism \eqref{HAn1}. 
Claim $\mathrm{(c)}$ also follows, since for $q=2$, 
the only possible summand on the right-hand side of the isomorphism \eqref{HAn1} 
is $H^{(2)}_0(\Gamma[z])$, which is zero since $C^{(2)}_0(\Gamma[z])=0$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corr-2: body_md -->
\label{Arn1} 
For $n\geqslant 2$, there are isomorphisms: 
\[ 
H^0(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{Q})\cong H^1(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{Q})\cong\mathbb{Q}, 
\qquad H^q(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{Q})\cong 0\quad\text{if\; $q\geqslant 2$}. 
\] 
In particular, for $q\geqslant 2$, the groups $H^q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_n\bigr)$ are finite.
<!-- end corr-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The map 
$\Gamma[z]\otimes\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}[y]$, $\,z^{(2r)}\to\frac{y^{r}}{r!}$, where $w(y)=2$, 
is a graded $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra isomorphism. 
Since $H_*(\mathbb{Q}[y];\mathbb{Q})\cong\mathbb{Q}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits\mathbb{Q}\cdot y$, we have: 
\[ 
H_q^{(2r)}(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{Q})\cong H_q^{(2r)}(\mathbb{Q}[y];\mathbb{Q})\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb{Q}&\text{if $(r,q)=(0,0),(1,1)$},\\ 
0&\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
Applying the functor $-\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}$ to 
isomorphism~\eqref{HAn1}, we obtain the desired result.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- defnr-10: body_md -->
For $n\geqslant0$, define the \emph{stabilization operator} 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}:\mathrm A(n)\longrightarrow \mathrm A(n-1) 
\] 
as follows. For $n=0$, this is the zero map 
$\mathrm A(0)\to \mathrm A(-1)=0$. For $n\geqslant1$, put 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}\bigl(e(n_1,\ldots,n_a)\bigr)= 
\begin{cases} 
e(n_1,\ldots,n_{a-1}), & \text{if } n_a=1,\\ 
0, & \text{if } n_a>1. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
 
Here, for $a=1$ and $n_1=1$, the expression 
$e(n_1,\ldots,n_{a-1})$ means the empty composition 
$e(0)=1\in \mathrm A(0)$.
<!-- end defnr-10 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{SeqS} 
For $n\geqslant 0$ and $q\geqslant 0$, there is a split short exact sequence 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow 
H^{(n)}_{n-q}\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr) 
\longrightarrow H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}(n)\bigr) 
\stackrel{\mathrm{St}^*}\relbar\joinrel\longrightarrow H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}(n-1)\bigr) 
\longrightarrow 0. 
\] 
Thus, there exists a canonical isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}(n)\bigr)\cong 
H^{(n)}_{n-q}\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}(n-1)\bigr). 
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For $n=0,1$, the assertion follows immediately from the 
definition of $\mathrm{St}$ in these cases. 
 
Let $n\geqslant 2$. 
For $0\leqslant 2r\leqslant n$, define 
\[ 
\Psi_{n,r}: 
H_{2r-q}^{(2r)}(\Gamma[z]) 
\longrightarrow H^q(\mathrm A(n)), 
\qquad 
[c]\longmapsto[c*e(1_{n-2r})]. 
\] 
Here the shuffle product is followed by the multiplication 
isomorphism 
$\Gamma[z]\otimes\Lambda[e(1)]\cong\mathrm E[z]$ 
and the identification of Theorem~\ref{SEF}. 
By the Eilenberg--Zilber theorem, these maps give an isomorphism 
\[ 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{0\leqslant 2r\leqslant n} 
H_{2r-q}^{(2r)}(\Gamma[z]) 
\stackrel{\cong}{\longrightarrow} 
H^q(\mathrm A(n)), 
\] 
where groups in negative homological degrees are understood 
to be zero. 
 
Every letter of a chain $c\in C_*(\Gamma[z])$ has positive 
even weight. Hence, for $a\geqslant1$, the shuffle terms 
in $c*e(1_a)$ ending in $e(1)$ correspond, with the same 
signs, to the terms in $c*e(1_{a-1})$. Consequently, 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}\bigl(c*e(1_a)\bigr)= 
\begin{cases} 
c*e(1_{a-1}),&a\geqslant1,\\ 
0,&a=0. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
Thus, 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}^*\Psi_{n,r}= 
\begin{cases} 
\Psi_{n-1,r},&2r<n,\\ 
0,&2r=n. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
It follows that $\mathrm{St}^*$ is surjective and its kernel is 
the summand $H_{n-q}^{(n)}(\Gamma[z])$. 
 
The canonical embedding 
\[ 
i_{n-1}^*:H^q(\mathrm A(n-1))\hookrightarrow H^q(\mathrm A(n)) 
\] 
introduced earlier maps the $r$-th summand of $H^q(\mathrm A(n-1))$ 
identically to the $r$-th summand of $H^q(\mathrm A(n))$. In terms of our basis, this means: 
\[ 
i_{n-1}^*\Psi_{n-1,r}([c])=\Psi_{n,r}([c]). 
\] 
Because $\mathrm{St}^*\Psi_{n,r}=\Psi_{n-1,r}$, it immediately 
follows that $\mathrm{St}^*\circ i_{n-1}^*=\mathrm{id}$. 
Thus, $i_{n-1}^*$ is a canonical section for $\mathrm{St}^*$, 
which proves that the short exact sequence splits.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{StabSH} 
For $n\geqslant 0$ the canonical map 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}^*:H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}(n)\bigr)\longrightarrow H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}(n-1)\bigr) 
\] 
is a surjection, and is an isomorphism if $n\geqslant\max\{3,2q-1\}$. 
In particular, the cohomology of the braid family $\mathbf B$ stabilizes.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Surjectivity follows from Theorem~\ref{SeqS}. 
Suppose that $n\geqslant\max\{3,2q-1\}$. 
By the same theorem, it suffices to show that 
$H_{n-q}^{(n)}(\Gamma[z])=0$. 
For odd $n$, this follows from the weight grading. 
For even $n$, put $r=n/2$. Then $r\geqslant q$ and $r\geqslant2$. 
If $r>q$, the corresponding chain group is zero. 
If $r=q$, then $q\geqslant2$, and the vanishing follows 
from the proof of Theorem~\ref{HGIso}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corr-3: body_md -->
\label{A2} 
Define 
\[ 
\mathrm A_2(n):= 
\begin{cases} 
\mathrm A(0),&\text{if }n=0,\\ 
0,&\text{if }n=1,\\ 
\mathrm{Ker}\bigl(\mathrm{St}:\mathrm A(n)\to\mathrm A(n-1)\bigr), 
&\text{if }n\geqslant2. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
For all $n,q\geqslant0$, there is a canonical isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q(\mathrm A_2(n)) 
\cong H_{n-q}^{(n)}(\Gamma[z]). 
\] 
For $n\geqslant2$, this gives 
\[ 
H^q(\mathrm A_2(n)) 
\cong\mathrm{Ker}(\mathrm{St}^*) 
\cong 
H^q(\mathbf B_n)\big/H^q(\mathbf B_{n-1}). 
\] 
In particular, for $0\leqslant n\leqslant2$, 
\[ 
H^q(\mathrm A_2(n))\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb Z,&(n,q)=(0,0)\text{ or }(n,q)=(2,1),\\ 
0,&\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
For $n\geqslant2$, the identifications follow from the 
long exact cohomology sequence associated with 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow\mathrm A_2(n) 
\longrightarrow\mathrm A(n) 
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{St}}\mathrm A(n-1) 
\longrightarrow0 
\] 
and the surjectivity in Theorem~\ref{SeqS}. 
The cases $n=0,1$ follow directly from the definitions.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lmr-3: body_md -->
\label{Zp} 
For any prime $p$, there is an isomorphism of graded algebras 
\[ 
H_*\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\cong\mathrm{E}_p[t],\quad 
\text{where}\quad\mathrm{E}_p[t]:=\mathrm{E}[t]\otimes\mathbb{F}_p, 
\] 
and 
$H_q\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ is generated by the cycle 
$t^{(q)}:=\Pi[t,t^{p-1}:q]$, the alternating product $\bigl[t\mid t^{p-1}\mid t\mid\dots\bigr]$ 
of $t$ and $t^{p-1}$ of total length $q>0$. 
In particular, $H_*\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ 
has the structure of a graded Hopf algebra with coproduct 
\[ 
\begin{cases} 
\Delta(t^{(2m)})&=\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i=0}^m t^{(2i)}\otimes t^{(2m-2i)},\\[2mm] 
\Delta(t^{(2m+1)})&=\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i=0}^m\bigl(t^{(2i)}\otimes t^{(2m+1-2i)}+t^{(2i+1)}\otimes t^{(2m-2i)}\bigr) 
\end{cases} 
\qquad\text{if $p>2$}, 
\] 
\[ 
\Delta(t^{(q)})=\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i=0}^q t^{(i)}\otimes t^{(q-i)}\qquad\text{if $p=2$}. 
\] 
In these formulas, $t^{(r)}$ denotes the homology 
class of the corresponding cycle for every $r\geqslant0$, 
with $t^{(0)}=1$ represented by the empty chain.
<!-- end lmr-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
A basis of $C_*\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ consists of chains 
$\bigl[t^{i_1}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigr]$, where $1\leqslant i_j\leqslant p-1$ for all $j$, 
and its differential is given by 
\[ 
d\bigl[t^{i_1}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigr]= 
\sum_{a=1}^{q-1}(-1)^a 
\bigl[t^{i_1}|\dots|t^{i_a+i_{a+1}}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigr]. 
\] 
Here a term with $i_a+i_{a+1}\geqslant p$ is understood to be zero. 
 
The isomorphism $H_q\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\cong\mathbb{F}_p\cdot t^{(q)}$ 
is evident for $p=2$, or when $q=0,1$. 
To prove it for $p>2$ and $q\geqslant 2$, we proceed by induction on $q$. 
 
Define an operator 
$h:C_q\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\to C_{q+1}\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ 
by setting 
\[ 
h\bigl[t^{i_1}|t^{i_2}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigr]:= 
\begin{cases} 
0&\text{if\; $i_1=1$},\\ 
\bigl[t|t^{i_1-1}|t^{i_2}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigl]&\text{if\; $i_1>1$}. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
A straightforward calculation yields the identities: 
\begin{align*} 
(hd+dh)\bigl[t^{i_1}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigr]&=-\bigl[t^{i_1}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigr] 
+(\text{terms starting with } t) \quad \text{for } i_1 > 1,\\ 
(hd+dh)[t|t^{i_2}|\dots|t^{i_q}] &=  
\begin{cases} 
-\bigl[t|t^{i_2}|\dots|t^{i_q}\bigr] & \text{if } i_2 \neq p-1,\\ 
0 & \text{if } i_2=p-1. 
\end{cases} 
\end{align*} 
If $z$ is a cycle, $dz=0$, so the first identity implies $z=-dh(z)+(\text{terms starting with } t)$. 
Since $dh(z)$ is a boundary, $z$ is homologous to a cycle $z'$ consisting entirely of terms starting with $t$. 
Writing $z'=A+B$, where $B$ consists of terms starting with 
$[t|t^{p-1}]$ and $A$ consists of terms starting with $[t|t^{i_2}]$ 
for $i_2 \neq p-1$, we apply $hd$ to $z'$. 
Since $z'$ is a cycle, $hd(z')=0$. By the second identity, $hd(B)=0$ and $hd(A)=-A$, 
which forces $A=0$. Thus, $z'$ consists exclusively of terms in $B$, 
showing that any cycle is homologous to a~cycle of the form $[t|t^{p-1}|z_1]$, 
where $z_1\in C_{q-2}\bigl(\mathbb{F}_p[t]\big/(t^p);\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ and $d(z_1)=0$. 
 
To verify that no nonzero class is lost, set 
$P:=\mathrm{id}+hd+dh$. 
Then for $q\geqslant2$, 
\[ 
P[t^{i_1}|\dots|t^{i_q}] 
= 
\begin{cases} 
[t|t^{p-1}|t^{i_3}|\dots|t^{i_q}], 
& i_1+i_2=p,\\ 
0,& i_1+i_2\ne p. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
Since $P$ commutes with $d$ and fixes every chain beginning 
with $[t|t^{p-1}]$, a boundary 
$[t|t^{p-1}|z_1]=dv$ satisfies 
\[ 
[t|t^{p-1}|z_1]=d(Pv) 
=[t|t^{p-1}|dv_1] 
\] 
for some $v_1$. Hence $z_1=dv_1$. 
Together with the preceding reduction, this proves that 
prefixing $[t|t^{p-1}]$ induces an isomorphism 
$H_{q-2}\cong H_q$ for $q\geqslant2$. 
The claimed description now follows by induction. 
 
The Pontryagin product of the homology classes 
of the cycles $t^{(q_1)}$ and $t^{(q_2)}$ 
corresponds to the homology class of the cycle $t^{(q_1)}*t^{(q_2)}$, 
where $*$ is the shuffle product (see \ref{EZ} and \ref{ttth2}). 
The equality 
\[ 
t^{(2a)}*t^{(2b)}=\pi(2a,2b)t^{(2a+2b)} 
\] 
is proved by a straightforward induction on $a$. 
Moreover, $t^{(2a+1)}*t^{(2b+1)}=0$. 
Indeed, this product contains the factor $t^{(1)}*t^{(1)}$, and 
$t^{(1)}*t^{(1)}=[t]*[t]=[t|t]-[t|t]=0$ for every prime $p$. 
Finally, by associativity, 
\[ 
t^{(2a+1)}*t^{(2b)}= 
t^{(2b)}*t^{(2a+1)}= 
\pi(2a+1,2b)t^{(2a+2b+1)}. 
\] 
This follows since $t^{(2a+1)}=t^{(2a)}*t^{(1)}$. 
 
Thus the Pontryagin product is given by 
$t^{(i)}*t^{(j)}=\pi(i,j)t^{(i+j)}$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{th1} 
For any prime $p$, there is a~canonical isomorphism of algebras 
\[ 
H_*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\;\cong\;\mathbin{\scalebox{1.1}{$\bigotimes$}}_{r\geqslant 0}\;\mathrm{E}_p[z_{p^r}], 
\] 
which endows $H_*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ with the structure of a~bigraded Hopf algebra. 
The bigrading of the right-hand side is defined as follows: 
\begin{align*} 
\deg\bigl(z_{p^{r_1}}^{(q_1)}\otimes{\dots}\otimes z_{p^{r_a}}^{(q_a)}\bigr)&:=q_1+\dots+q_a,\\[1mm] 
 w\bigl(z_{p^{r_1}}^{(q_1)}\otimes{\dots}\otimes z_{p^{r_a}}^{(q_a)}\bigr)&:= 
 w\bigl(z_{p^{r_1}}^{(q_1)}\bigr)+\dots+ w\bigl(z_{p^{r_a}}^{(q_a)}\bigr), 
\end{align*} 
with 
\[ 
w\bigl(z_{p^r}^{(q)}\bigr):= 
\begin{cases} 
\frac{q}{2}\, p^{r+1} w(z)&\text{if}\quad q\equiv 0\mod 2,\\[2mm] 
\frac{q-1}{2}\, p^{r+1} w(z)+p^r w(z)&\text{if}\quad q\equiv 1\mod 2. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
Under the above isomorphism, the monomials 
$x=z_{p^{r_1}}^{(q_1)}\otimes{\dots}\otimes z_{p^{r_a}}^{(q_a)}$ 
with $\deg(x)=m$ and $ w(x)=n$ form a basis of the 
$\mathbb F_p$-vector space 
$H^{(n)}_m\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb F_p\bigr)$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{corHP} 
For a~prime $p$, there is an isomorphism of bigraded primitively generated Hopf algebras 
\[ 
H^*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\Lambda_p[x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots]\otimes\mathbb{F}_p[y_0,y_1,y_2,\dots] 
&\text{if\; $p>2$},\\[1mm] 
\mathbb{F}_2[x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots]&\text{if\; 
$p=2$}, 
\end{cases} 
\] 
where $\deg(x_r)=1,\,\deg(y_r)=2,\, w(x_r)=w(z)p^r,\, w(y_r)=w(z)p^{r+1}$, 
and the bigrading on cohomology 
is dual to the bigrading on homology from Theorem~\ref{th1}.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{CHGZ} 
There is an isomorphism of groups 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb Z, & q=0,1,\\[2mm] 
\displaystyle\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_p 
\beta_p\bigl(H^{q-1}(\Gamma[z];\mathbb F_p)\bigr), 
& q\geqslant 2, 
\end{cases} 
\] 
where the sum runs over all primes $p$, and 
$\beta_p:H^{q-1}\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb F_p\bigr) 
\longrightarrow H^q\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)$ 
is the Bockstein homomorphism associated with the exact sequence of 
coefficients 
$0\longrightarrow \mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times p} 
\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\mathbb F_p\longrightarrow 0$. 
 
Let 
$b_p^*:H^{*-1}\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb F_p\bigr) 
\longrightarrow H^*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb F_p\bigr)$ 
be the mod-$p$ Bockstein differential dual to the homological 
Bockstein associated with the exact sequence 
$0\longrightarrow \mathbb F_p\longrightarrow \mathbb Z_{p^2} 
\longrightarrow \mathbb F_p\longrightarrow 0$. 
Then $b_p^*$ is the graded derivation given by 
\begin{equation}\label{Bockp} 
\begin{split} 
b^*_p(x_0)=0,&\qquad b^*_p(x_r)=y_{r-1}\quad (r\geqslant 1), 
\qquad b^*_p(y_r)=0\quad (r\geqslant 0),\quad\text{if $p>2$,}{}\\ 
&b^*_2(x_0)=0,\qquad b^*_2(x_r)=x_{r-1}^2\quad (r>0). 
\end{split} 
\end{equation} 
Moreover, the group $H^*\bigl(\Gamma[z]\bigr)$ is squarefree-torsion.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $b_p:H_*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\to H_{*-1}\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ 
denote the Bockstein homomorphism associated with the exact sequence of coefficients 
$0\to\mathbb{F}_p\to\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}\to\mathbb{F}_p\to 0$. 
The definition of $b_p$ implies that for $r\geqslant 0$, we have 
\[ 
b_p\bigl(z_{p^r}^{(0)}\bigr)=0,\qquad b_p\bigl(z_{p^r}^{(1)}\bigr)=0,\qquad 
b_p\bigl(z_{p^r}^{(2)}\bigr)=z_{p^{r+1}}^{(1)}. 
\] 
Consequently, for the homomorphism  
$b_p^*:H^{*-1}\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\to H^*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ 
dual to $b_p$, the action of $b_p^*$ is given by formulas~\eqref{Bockp}. 
 
Since $b_p^*$ is a~graded derivation, these formulas determine its 
action on $H^*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ by virtue of Theorem~\ref{corHP}. 
Let $BH^*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ denote the 
cohomology of the complex $H^*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ 
with differential~$b_p^*$. 
The formulas \eqref{Bockp} easily imply that for each $p$, 
\[ 
BH^*\bigl(\Gamma[z];\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\cong\mathbb{F}_p\oplus\mathbb{F}_px_0. 
\] 
All these calculations respect weights. For each fixed 
weight, the integral chain complex is a bounded complex 
of finitely generated free abelian groups. We therefore 
apply the Bockstein criterion separately in each weight. 
 
In each weight and cohomological degree, the Bockstein 
cohomology has the same dimension over $\mathbb F_p$ 
as the rational cohomology over $\mathbb Q$. 
The remaining claims therefore follow from the Bockstein 
criterion (see \cite[Cor.~3.E.4]{Hatcher}).
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{corth1} 
For any prime $p$, there is an isomorphism of bigraded 
$\mathbb F_p$-vector spaces 
\[ 
H^*\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr) 
\cong 
\mathop{\textstyle\bigotimes}\nolimits_{r=0}^\infty \mathrm{E}_p[z_{p^r}]. 
\] 
The right-hand side carries the Hopf algebra structure described in 
Theorem~\ref{th1}; under the above identification this gives the 
algebraic structure used below. 
The monomials 
\[ 
h=z_{p^{r_1}}^{(q_1)}\otimes{\dots}\otimes z_{p^{r_m}}^{(q_m)}, 
\qquad 
0\leqslant r_1<\cdots<r_m,\quad q_i>0, 
\] 
where $w(h)-\deg(h)=q$ and $w(h)\leqslant n$, 
form a basis of 
$H^q(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb F_p)\subset 
H^q(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb F_p)$.\footnote{Here and below, empty products are allowed and represent the unit.}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{corHP00} 
For any prime $p$, there is an isomorphism of bigraded 
primitively generated Hopf algebras 
\[ 
H_*\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\Lambda_p[x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots]\otimes\mathbb{F}_p[y_0,y_1,y_2,\dots] 
&\quad\mbox{if}\quad p>2,\\[1mm] 
\mathbb{F}_2[x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots]&\quad\mbox{if}\quad p=2, 
\end{cases} 
\] 
where $\deg(x_r)=2p^r-1,\;\deg(y_r)=2p^{r+1}-2,\; w(x_r)=2p^r,\; w(y_r)=2p^{r+1}$. 
A basis of $H_q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\subset H_q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ 
is given by the set of monomials 
\[ 
h= 
\begin{cases} 
x_{i_1}\wedge\dots\wedge x_{i_a}\otimes y_{j_1}^{r_1}\cdots y_{j_b}^{r_b}&\text{if $p>2$},\\[1mm] 
x_{i_1}^{r_1}\cdots x_{i_a}^{r_a}&\text{if $p=2$}, 
\end{cases} 
\quad\text{where\;\; $i_1<\cdots<i_a,\;\; j_1<\cdots<j_b,\;\; r_\ell>0$}, 
\] 
and $\deg(h)=q$, $ w(h)\leqslant n$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{HGZ0} 
There is an isomorphism of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules 
\[ 
H_q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty\bigr)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb{Z}&\text{if\; $q=0,1$},\\[1mm] 
\bigoplus_p\beta_p\bigl(H_{q+1}(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p)\bigr)&\text{if\; 
$q\geqslant 2$}, 
\end{cases} 
\] 
where the sum runs over all primes $p$, and $\beta_p$ denotes the 
homological Bockstein homomorphism associated with the exact sequence 
of coefficients 
$0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times p}\mathbb Z 
\longrightarrow\mathbb F_p\longrightarrow 0$. 
Under the isomorphism of Theorem~\ref{corHP00}, the corresponding 
mod-$p$ Bockstein differential on $H_*(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb F_p)$ 
is given by formulas~\eqref{Bockp}. 
 
For $n\geqslant2$, one also has 
$H_0(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong H_1(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong\mathbb Z$, 
and for $q\geqslant 2$, 
\[ 
H_q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_n\bigr)\cong\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_p\beta_p\bigl(H_{q+1}(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{F}_p)\bigr). 
\]
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{HGZB} 
There is an isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty\bigr)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb{Z}&\text{if\; 
$q=0,1$},\\[1mm] 
\bigoplus_p\beta_p^*\bigl(H^{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p)\bigr)&\text{if\; $q\geqslant 2$}, 
\end{cases} 
\] 
where the sum runs over all primes $p$, and $\beta_p^*$ 
denotes the Bockstein homomorphism on cohomologies associated with the exact sequence 
of coefficients 
$0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times p}\mathbb Z 
\longrightarrow\mathbb F_p\longrightarrow 0$. 
Moreover, the group $H^q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty\bigr)$ is squarefree-torsion. For $q\geqslant 2$, we have: 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_n\bigr)\cong\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_p\beta_p^*\bigl(H^{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{F}_p)\bigr). 
\]
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- remnr-2: body_md -->
\label{SegE} 
Segal's results \cite{Seg} identify the stable cohomology 
of braid groups, with its cup product, with the cohomology 
of $\Omega^2S^3$. For an explicit description of 
$H_*(\Omega^2S^3)$, see 
\cite[Cor.~10.26.4]{AlgMeth}. 
 
The agreement of the additive groups and Bockstein 
operators supports the expectation that the multiplication 
obtained here from the algebraic Pontryagin product agrees 
with this cup product. However, compatibility of our 
identifications with multiplication is not established 
by the present argument. 
It would be desirable to recover the cup product directly 
from the Fuchs complex and thereby establish this 
compatibility within the algebraic approach developed here.
<!-- end remnr-2 -->
<!-- corr-4: body_md -->
\label{CoBn} 
Denote by $H_q^{(w)}\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ the $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector subspace 
of $H_q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)$ spanned by all homology classes of weight $w$. 
Then for any prime $p$, we have: 
\[ 
\mathcal{H}_p(t, u):=\sum_{q\geqslant 0}\sum_{w\geqslant 0}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}  
H_q^{(w)}\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\,u^wt^q= 
\prod_{r\geqslant 0}\frac{1+u^{2p^r}t^{2p^r-1}}{1-u^{2p^{r+1}}t^{2p^{r+1}-2}}. 
\] 
Moreover, for any $n\geqslant 1$, let\; $\mathcal{H}_p(t, u)=1+\sum_{q=1}^\infty f_q(u)t^q$. Then 
\[ 
\mathrm{H}_{p,n}(t):=\sum_{q\geqslant 0} 
\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H_q(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{F}_p)t^q= 
1+\sum_{0<q\leqslant n}\bigl(f_q(u)\bmod u^{n+1}\bigr)\Big|_{u=1}t^q. 
\] 
In particular, by Arnold's stability theorem, 
\[ 
\mathrm{H}_p(t):=\sum_{q\geqslant 0} 
\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p} H_q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\,t^q= 
\prod_{r\geqslant 0}\;\frac{1+t^{2p^r-1}}{1-t^{2p^{r+1}-2}}. 
\]
<!-- end corr-4 -->
<!-- lmr-4: body_md -->
\label{HoB} 
For any prime $p$ and $n\geqslant 2$, we have the following identities: 
\begin{align} 
\sum_{q\geqslant 0} 
\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\big(H_q(\mathbf{B}_n)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p\big)t^q 
&= 
t+\frac{1}{1+t}\mathrm{H}_{p,n}(t),\label{eqh1}\\ 
\sum_{q\geqslant 0}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\big(H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p\big)t^q 
&= 
1+\frac{t}{1+t}\mathrm{H}_{p,n}(t).\label{eqh2} 
\end{align}
<!-- end lmr-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Set 
$ 
h_p(q,n):=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p} H_q(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{F}_p),\; 
\overline{h}_p(q,n):=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\bigl(H_q(\mathbf{B}_n)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p\bigr). 
$ 
For brevity, for fixed $p$ and $n$, we use the shorthand 
$a_q:=h_p(q,n)$ and $b_q:=\overline{h}_p(q,n)$, 
and let $\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t)$ be the left-hand side of identity \eqref{eqh1}. 
 
For any prime $p$ and $q\geqslant 0$, the universal coefficient theorem yields the short exact sequence 
\[ 
0\to H_q(\mathbf{B}_n)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p\to H_q(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{F}_p) 
\to\mathrm{Tor}\bigl(H_{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_n),\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\to 0. 
\] 
It shows that 
$ 
a_q=b_q+\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\mathrm{Tor}\bigl(H_{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_n),\mathbb{F}_p\bigr). 
$ 
Since $H_0(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong H_1(\mathbf{B}_n)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ and the groups $H_q(\mathbf{B}_n)$ 
are squarefree-torsion for $q\geqslant 2$, this expression implies: 
\begin{gather*} 
a_0=b_0=1,\quad a_1=b_1=1,\quad a_2=b_2,\quad 
a_q=b_{q-1}+b_q\quad\text{for $q\geqslant 3$}. 
\end{gather*} 
Thus, 
\begin{multline*} 
\mathrm{H}_{p,n}(t)=1+t+b_2t^2+\sum_{q=3}^{\infty}(b_{q-1}+b_q)t^q\\ 
=t\Big(\sum_{q=2}^{\infty}b_qt^q\Big)+\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t) 
=t\big(\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t)-1-t\big)+\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t)= 
(1+t)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t)-t(1+t). 
\end{multline*} 
From this expression, identity \eqref{eqh1} follows. 
 
Since the groups $H_q(\mathbf{B}_n)$ are squarefree-torsion, 
from the universal coefficient theorem we obtain a (non-canonical) splitting 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathbf{B}_n\bigr)\cong\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(H_q(\mathbf{B}_n),\mathbb{Z}\bigr)\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits\mathrm{Ext}\bigl(H_{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_n),\mathbb{Z}\bigr) 
\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb{Z}&\text{if } q=0,1,\\ 
0&\text{if } q=2,\\ 
H_{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_n)&\text{if } q\geqslant 3. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
Tensoring this isomorphism with $\mathbb{F}_p$ yields that 
$\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\bigl(H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)=b_{q-1}$ for $q\geqslant 3$. 
For $q\in\{0,1,2\}$, the dimensions are $1,1$, and $0$, respectively. 
Multiplying by $t^q$ and summing over all $q \geqslant 0$ gives: 
\begin{multline*} 
\sum_{q\geqslant 0}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}\big(H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p\big)t^q 
=1+t+\sum_{q=3}^{\infty} b_{q-1}t^q \\ 
=1+t+t\Big(\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}b_jt^j\Big) 
=1+t+t\big(\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t)-1-t\big) 
=1-t^2+t\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t). 
\end{multline*} 
Substituting $\overline{\mathrm{H}}_{p,n}(t)=t+\frac{1}{1+t}\mathrm{H}_{p,n}(t)$ 
from \eqref{eqh1} yields identity \eqref{eqh2}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remnr-3: body_md -->
\label{Steenrod} 
Interestingly, for any prime $p$, the generating function $\mathrm{H}_p(t)$ for the sequence 
$\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}H_q(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p)$ 
coincides with the graded dimension of the Steenrod algebra 
$\mathcal{A}_p$. However, $H_*(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p)$ 
and $\mathcal{A}_p$ are not isomorphic as Hopf algebras. Indeed, 
$H_*(\mathbf{B}_\infty;\mathbb{F}_p)$ is a primitively generated 
Hopf algebra, whereas neither $\mathcal{A}_p$ nor its dual has this property; 
see~\cite{Milnor}.
<!-- end remnr-3 -->
<!-- lmr-5: body_md -->
\label{ACnT} 
For $n\geqslant 1$, there is a canonical isomorphism of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{C}(n)\cong\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{r\geqslant 0}\mathrm{A}(n-r)\times y^r,\qquad\text{where}\qquad 
\mathrm{C}^q(n)\cong\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{r\geqslant 0}\mathrm{A}^{q-r}(n-r)\times y^r, 
\] 
such that $\partial_C(c\times y^r)=\partial(c)\times y^r$ for $c\in\mathrm{A}(n-r)$.
<!-- end lmr-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The claimed isomorphism of modules follows directly from the definition above. 
The formula $\partial_C(c\times y^r)=\partial(c)\times y^r$ 
for the basis cochains follows from the definition of the Salvetti complex, 
since for basis elements this definition shows that 
\[ 
\partial_C\bigl(e(n_1,\dots,n_a)\times y^r\bigr)= 
\partial\bigl(e(n_1,\dots,n_a)\bigr)\times y^r. 
\] 
This follows from the formula 
\begin{equation}\label{CC} 
\left.\frac{C_{n_a+r}(t)}{A_{n_a-1}(t)\cdot C_r(t)}\right|_{t=-1}=0, 
\end{equation} 
where $C_0(t)=A_0(t):=1$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{CohC} 
For $n\geqslant 1$, we have: 
\begin{equation}\label{HCn} 
H^q\bigl(\mathbf{C}_n\bigr)\cong\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{r\geqslant 0}H^{q-r}\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{n-r}\bigr). 
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{StabS_C} 
For $n\geqslant 2$, there is a canonical morphism of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_C:\mathrm{C}(n)\longrightarrow\mathrm{C}(n-1) 
\] 
such that, for any $q\geqslant 1$, the induced homomorphism 
$ 
\mathrm{St}^*_C:H^q(\mathbf{C}_n)\longrightarrow H^q(\mathbf{C}_{n-1}) 
$ 
is surjective, and is an isomorphism if $n\geqslant\max\{q+2,2q-1\}$. 
Thus, the cohomology of the family $\mathbf{C}$ stabilizes.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
For $0\leqslant r\leqslant n$ and $c\in\mathrm{A}(n-r)$, set  
$\mathrm{St}_C(c\times y^r)=\mathrm{St}(c)\times y^r$. Then Lemma~\ref{ACnT} implies that 
$\mathrm{St}_C$ defines the declared morphism of complexes. 
For $q\geqslant 0$, the map 
\[ 
H^q(\mathrm{C}(n))\stackrel{\mathrm{St}^*_C}\relbar\joinrel\longrightarrow H^q(\mathrm{C}(n-1)) 
\] 
is induced by the set of maps 
\begin{equation}\label{r} 
H^{q-r}(\mathrm{A}(n-r))\stackrel{\mathrm{St}^*}\relbar\joinrel\longrightarrow H^{q-r}(\mathrm{A}(n-r-1)), 
\end{equation} 
where $r\geqslant 0$. 
Since Theorem~\ref{StabSH} imply that $\mathrm{St}^*$ is surjective for all $r\geqslant0$, 
the map $\mathrm{St}^*_C$ is surjective as well. 
If $q\geqslant 2$ and $n\geqslant 2q-1$, then $n-r\geqslant 2(q-r)-1$ for any $r\geqslant 0$. 
Theorem \ref{StabSH} shows that the map \eqref{r} is an isomorphism if $q-r\geqslant 2$. 
For $q-r\in\{0,1\}$ the maps 
\[ 
H^1(\mathrm{A}(n-q+1))\stackrel{\mathrm{St}^*}\longrightarrow H^1(\mathrm{A}(n-q))\qquad\text{and} 
\qquad H^0(\mathrm{A}(n-q))\stackrel{\mathrm{St}^*}\longrightarrow H^0(\mathrm{A}(n-q-1)) 
\] 
are both isomorphisms only if $n\geqslant q+2$. The proof is completed.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corr-5: body_md -->
\label{StabC} 
The stable cohomology of the family $\mathbf{C}$ is given by the isomorphism: 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathbf{C}_\infty\bigr)\cong\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{r\geqslant 0}H^{q-r}(\mathbf{B}_\infty). 
\] 
Thus, for any prime $p$, as well as for $p=0$, we have: 
\[ 
\mathrm{G}_p\bigl(\mathbf{C}_\infty;t\bigr)= 
\frac{1}{1-t}\;\mathrm{G}_p(\mathbf{B}_\infty;t). 
\]
<!-- end corr-5 -->
<!-- corr-6: body_md -->
\label{DC} 
For $n\geqslant 2$, we have 
\[ 
\dim_{\mathbb{Q}} H^q\bigl(\mathbf{C}_n;\mathbb{Q}\bigr)= 
\begin{cases} 
1&\text{if $q=0$ or $q=n$},\\ 
2&\text{if $1\leqslant q<n$},\\ 
0&\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-6 -->
<!-- lmr-6: body_md -->
\label{HCA} 
For $n\geqslant3$, there is an isomorphism of complexes 
\[ 
\widetilde{\mathrm{C}}(n)\cong 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{m\geqslant 1} 
\mathrm A(n-m)^{\oplus m},\qquad\text{where} 
\qquad\widetilde{\mathrm{C}}^q(n)\cong 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{m\geqslant 1} 
\mathrm A^{q-m+1}(n-m)^{\oplus m}. 
\]
<!-- end lmr-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $l,r\geqslant0$ be fixed. Consider the submodule 
\[ 
D_{l,r}(n):= 
x^l\times \mathrm A(n-l-r-1)\times y^r 
\subset \widetilde{\mathrm{C}}(n). 
\] 
Here $0\leqslant l+r\leqslant n-1$. 
 
The possible boundary terms which join the middle $A$-part to the left 
or to the right terminal block vanish by the same calculation as in 
formula~\eqref{CC}. Hence the differential preserves $D_{l,r}(n)$. 
Before changing signs, it is given by 
\[ 
\partial_{\widetilde C} 
\bigl(x^l\times c\times y^r\bigr) 
= 
(-1)^l x^l\times \partial(c)\times y^r, 
\qquad 
c\in \mathrm A(n-l-r-1).\footnote{We shall use the following elementary observation. If $K$ is a 
cochain complex, then the complexes $(K,d)$ and $(K,-d)$ are 
isomorphic, via $c\mapsto (-1)^{\deg(c)}c$. More generally, a 
constant factor $(-1)^l$ in the differential on a fixed summand can 
be removed by the automorphism $c\mapsto (-1)^{l\deg(c)}c$.} 
\] 
The factor $(-1)^l$ appears because the differential on the middle 
$A$-part is shifted past the $l$ vertices in the left terminal block. 
By the elementary observation in the footnote, this constant factor 
$(-1)^l$ can be removed by a degree-wise automorphism. Thus 
$D_{l,r}(n)$ is identified with the usual complex 
$\mathrm A(n-l-r-1)$, shifted in degree by $l+r$. 
 
Set $m=l+r+1$. For a fixed $m$, where $1\leqslant m\leqslant n$, there are exactly 
$m$ pairs $(l,r)$ with $l+r=m-1$, namely 
\[ 
(l,r)=(0,m-1),(1,m-2),\ldots,(m-1,0). 
\] 
For each of these pairs we have $n-l-r-1=n-m$. 
Moreover, multiplication by $x^l$ and $y^r$ shifts the cohomological degree by $l+r=m-1$. 
 
Therefore a cochain $c\in \mathrm A^j(n-m)$ 
contributes to total degree $q=j+m-1$, or equivalently $j=q-m+1$. 
Hence 
\[ 
\widetilde{\mathrm{C}}^q(n)\cong 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{m\geqslant1} 
\mathrm A^{q-m+1}(n-m)^{\oplus m}. 
\] 
With respect to these identifications, the differential is the usual 
differential $\partial$ on each copy of $\mathrm A(n-m)$. 
This proves the claimed isomorphism of complexes.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{CohCC} 
For $n\geqslant3$, we have 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf C}_n\bigr)\cong 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{m\geqslant 1} 
H^{q-m+1}\bigl(\mathbf B_{n-m}\bigr)^{\oplus m}. 
\]
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{StabS_CC} 
For $n\geqslant 4$, there is a canonical morphism of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_{\widetilde C}:\widetilde{\mathrm{C}}(n) 
\longrightarrow 
\widetilde{\mathrm{C}}(n-1), 
\] 
such that for any $q\geqslant1$, the induced homomorphism 
$\mathrm{St}^*_{\widetilde C}: 
H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf C}_n)\longrightarrow 
H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf C}_{n-1})$ 
is surjective, and is an isomorphism if $n\geqslant\max\{q+4,2q\}$. 
Thus, the cohomology of the family $\widetilde{\mathbf C}$ stabilizes.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The proof is similar to that of Theorem~\ref{StabS_C}, 
with the following modifications. 
Under the decomposition of Lemma~\ref{HCA}, the morphism 
$\mathrm{St}_{\widetilde C}$ is induced on the summand 
$\mathrm A(n-m)$ by the stabilization map 
$\mathrm{St}:\mathrm A(n-m)\longrightarrow \mathrm A(n-m-1)$. 
Hence on cohomology it is induced by 
\[ 
H^{q-m+1}(\mathrm A(n-m)) 
\longrightarrow 
H^{q-m+1}(\mathrm A(n-m-1)). 
\] 
Put $d=q-m+1$ and $k=n-m$. 
Surjectivity follows from Theorem~\ref{StabSH}. 
For $d\geqslant2$, the inequality $n\geqslant2q$ 
implies $k\geqslant2d-1$, so the map is an 
isomorphism by the same theorem. 
For $d=0,1$, the assertion follows directly from 
the cohomology of braid groups in these degrees, 
using $n\geqslant q+4$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corr-7: body_md -->
\label{StabCC} 
The stable cohomology of the family $\widetilde{\mathbf{C}}$ is given by the isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf C}_\infty\bigr)\cong 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{m\geqslant1} 
\bigl(H^{q-m+1}(\mathbf B_\infty)\bigr)^{\oplus m}. 
\] 
Thus, for any prime $p$, as well as for $p=0$, we have 
\[ 
\mathrm G_p\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf C}_\infty;t\bigr)= 
\frac{1}{(1-t)^2}\, 
\mathrm G_p(\mathbf B_\infty;t). 
\]
<!-- end corr-7 -->
<!-- corr-8: body_md -->
\label{DCC} 
For $n\geqslant3$, we have 
\[ 
\dim_{\mathbb Q}H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf C}_n;\mathbb Q)= 
\begin{cases} 
2q+1, & \text{if $0\leqslant q\leqslant n-2$},\\ 
n, & \text{if $q=n-1$},\\ 
0, & \text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-8 -->
<!-- remnr-4: body_md -->
Corollary~\ref{StabC} shows that, as graded abelian groups, 
\[ 
H^*(\mathbf{C}_\infty)\cong 
H^*(\mathbf{B}_\infty)\otimes H^*(\Omega S^2). 
\] 
Similarly, Corollary~\ref{StabCC} shows that, as graded abelian groups, 
\[ 
H^*(\widetilde{\mathbf{C}}_\infty)\cong 
H^*(\mathbf{B}_\infty)\otimes H^*(\Omega S^2\times\Omega S^2). 
\] 
 
Note that in his 1974 paper \cite{FuchsQ}, Fuchs announced the existence of a homological 
equivalence between the spaces $K(\mathbf{C}_\infty,1)$ and $\Omega^2 S^3\times\Omega S^2$ 
(see Remark~\ref{SegE}).
<!-- end remnr-4 -->
<!-- defnr-11: body_md -->
\label{DefDr} 
Let $\mathrm{D}_r(n)$ denote the submodule of $\mathrm{D}(n)$ generated by the 
parabolic subgroups $P\subset D_n$ with $h(P)=r\geqslant 2$. 
We use the identification 
\[ 
\mathrm{D}_0(n)=\mathrm{A}(n),\qquad 
\mathrm{D}_r(n)=\mathrm{A}(n-r)\times y^r\quad\text{for } 2\leqslant r\leqslant n, 
\qquad 
\mathrm{D}_r(n)=0 \quad \text{for } r>n. 
\] 
For $i\geqslant 0$, define the submodule $\mathrm{T}_i(n)$ of $\mathrm{D}(n)$ by 
\[ 
\mathrm{T}_i(n):= 
\begin{cases} 
\mathrm{A}(n)+\sigma(\mathrm{A}(n))&\text{if $i=0$},\\ 
\mathrm{D}_{2i}(n)\oplus\mathrm{D}_{2i+1}(n)&\text{if $i\geqslant 1$}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end defnr-11 -->
<!-- lmr-7: body_md -->
\label{d00} 
For $n\geqslant 4$, the action of $\partial_D$ on 
$\mathrm{T}_0(n)$ is determined by the commutation relation 
$\partial_D\circ\sigma=\sigma\circ\partial_D$ and the formula 
\[ 
\partial_D(c)= 
\begin{cases} 
\partial(c)\mathbf{\dotplus}\sigma\bigl(\partial(c)\bigr)&\text{if $c\in\mathrm{A}_1(n)$},\\ 
\partial(c)&\text{if $c\in\mathrm{A}_2(n)$}. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
In particular, $\mathrm{T}_0(n)$ is a subcomplex of\, $\mathrm{D}(n)$.
<!-- end lmr-7 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For $c\in\mathrm{A}_1(n)$ the formula follows from the definition of $\partial_D$. 
 
For a basis cochain $c=e(n_1,\dots,n_a)\in\mathrm{A}_2(n)$, the definition of $\partial_D$ yields: 
\[ 
\partial_D(c)=\partial(c) 
+(-1)^a\left.\frac{D_{n_a}(t)}{A_{n_a-1}(t)}\right|_{t=-1} 
e(n_1,\dots,n_{a-1})\times y^{n_a} 
=\partial(c). 
\] 
This proves the formula for $c\in\mathrm{A}_2(n)$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lmr-8: body_md -->
\label{d0} 
For $n\geqslant 4$, there is a canonical isomorphism of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{T}_0(n)\cong\mathrm{A}(n)\oplus\mathrm{A}_2(n). 
\] 
Thus, for $n\geqslant 4$, we have the isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{T}_0(n)\bigr)\cong 
H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\oplus\left[H^q(\mathbf{B}_{n})\big/H^q(\mathbf{B}_{n-1})\right]. 
\]
<!-- end lmr-8 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Define 
\[ 
\Delta\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(n)\bigr):=\{\,c+\sigma(c)\mid c\in\mathrm{A}_2(n)\,\}. 
\] 
Then 
\[ 
\mathrm{T}_0(n) 
=\mathrm{A}_2(n)\oplus\mathrm{A}_1(n)\oplus\sigma\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(n)\bigr) 
=\mathrm{A}_1(n)\oplus\Delta\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(n)\bigr)\oplus\mathrm{A}_2(n). 
\] 
The formula for $\partial_D$ given in Lemma~\ref{d00} 
shows that $\mathrm{A}_1(n)\oplus\Delta\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(n)\bigr)$ is a subcomplex of 
$\mathrm{T}_0(n)$ isomorphic to $\mathrm{A}(n)$. 
Therefore, this decomposition of $\mathrm{T}_0(n)$ yields the claimed isomorphism. 
The final isomorphism follows from Corollary~\ref{A2}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lmr-9: body_md -->
\label{di} 
For a cochain $c\times y^r\in\mathrm{D}_r(n)$ with $c\in\mathrm{A}(n-r)$ and $r\geqslant 2$, we have 
\[ 
\partial_D(c\times y^r)= 
\partial(c)\times y^r+(-1)^{\deg(c)}\chi(r)\cdot\mathrm{St}(c)\times y^{r+1}, 
\] 
where $\chi(r):=1+(-1)^r$. 
Hence, for $i\geqslant 1$, $\mathrm{T}_i(n)$ is a subcomplex of $\mathrm{D}(n)$.
<!-- end lmr-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
It suffices to verify the lemma for the basis cochains $c=e(n_1,\dots,n_a)\in\mathrm{A}(n-r)$. 
The result then follows from the definition of $\partial_D$, together with the easily verified identity 
\[ 
\left.\frac{D_{n_a+r}(t)}{A_{n_a-1}(t)\cdot D_r(t)}\right|_{t=-1}= 
\begin{cases} 
0 &\text{if\; $n_a>1$},\\ 
\chi(r)\,&\text{if\; $n_a=1$}. 
\end{cases} 
\qedhere 
\]
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corr-9: body_md -->
\label{Sum} 
For $n\geqslant 4$, there is an isomorphism: 
\[ 
H^q(\mathrm{T}(n))\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{1\leqslant i\leqslant\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor}H^q(\mathrm{T}_i(n)) 
&\text{if $q<n$},\\[2mm] 
\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n-1)\mathbb{Z}&\text{if $q=n$}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-9 -->
<!-- lmr-10: body_md -->
\label{cone} 
Let $(K_0, d_0)$ and $(K_1, d_1)$ be cochain complexes, 
and let $V:K_0\longrightarrow K_1$ be a morphism of complexes. 
Consider the graded module $\mathrm{Cn}:=\bigoplus_m \mathrm{Cn}^m$, 
where $\mathrm{Cn}^m:=K_0^m\oplus K_1^{m-1}$. We equip $\mathrm{Cn}$ with a linear map 
$\partial_\mathrm{Cn}:\mathrm{Cn}\to \mathrm{Cn}$ whose restriction $\partial_m:\mathrm{Cn}^m\to \mathrm{Cn}^{m+1}$ is defined by 
\[ 
\partial_m(a,b):=\bigl(d_0(a),\,(-1)^m V(a)+d_1(b)\bigr). 
\] 
Then $\partial_\mathrm{Cn}$ defines a cochain complex structure on $\mathrm{Cn}$. 
Moreover, $\mathrm{Cn}$ fits into a long exact sequence in cohomology: 
\[ 
\cdots\longrightarrow H^{m-1}(K_0)\xrightarrow{\,V^*\,} H^{m-1}(K_1)\longrightarrow H^m(\mathrm{Cn}) 
\longrightarrow H^m(K_0)\xrightarrow{\,V^*\,} H^m(K_1)\longrightarrow\cdots. 
\]
<!-- end lmr-10 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Checking that $\partial^2_m=0$ is straightforward. 
 
Introduce the shifted subcomplex $K_1(-1)\subset \mathrm{Cn}$, defined by 
\[ 
K_1(-1)^m:=\{(0,c)\mid c\in K_1^{m-1}\}, 
\] 
with the differential induced from $\mathrm{Cn}$, that is, 
$d(0,c)=(0,d_1c)$. 
 
The natural inclusion and projection maps yield a short exact sequence of cochain complexes: 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow K_1(-1)\longrightarrow \mathrm{Cn}\longrightarrow K_0\longrightarrow 0. 
\] 
This sequence induces the declared long exact sequence in cohomology.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- defnr-12: body_md -->
The cochain complex $\mathrm{Cn}$ defined in Lemma~\ref{cone} is called the \emph{mapping cone} 
of the morphism of complexes $V:K_0\longrightarrow K_1$.
<!-- end defnr-12 -->
<!-- prr-1: body_md -->
\label{HTi00} 
For $k\geqslant 2$, let $\mathrm{Cn}(k)$ be the mapping cone of the morphism 
$2\,\mathrm{St}:\mathrm{A}(k)\to\mathrm{A}(k-1)$. Then, for every $m\geqslant0$, there is an isomorphism: 
\[ 
H^m\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\bigr)\cong H^m\bigl(\mathrm A_2(k)\bigr) 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits H^{m-1}\bigl(\mathrm A(k-1)\bigr)\otimes\mathbb Z_2 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits H^m\bigl(\mathrm A(k-1)\bigr)[2]. 
\]
<!-- end prr-1 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For $k=2$, the complexes $\mathrm A(2)$ and 
$\mathrm A(1)$ have zero differentials, with 
\[ 
\mathrm A^0(2)=\mathbb Z\cdot e(1,1),\qquad 
\mathrm A^1(2)=\mathbb Z\cdot e(2),\qquad 
\mathrm A^0(1)=\mathbb Z\cdot e(1). 
\] 
Since $\mathrm{St}(e(1,1))=e(1)$ and $\mathrm{St}(e(2))=0$, 
the cone $\mathrm{Cn}(2)$ is 
\[ 
\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\,a\mapsto(0,2a)\,} 
\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z, 
\] 
concentrated in degrees $0$ and $1$. Hence 
\[ 
H^m(\mathrm{Cn}(2))\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z_2,&m=1,\\ 
0,&m\ne1. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
This agrees with the asserted formula, since 
$\mathrm A_2(2)=\mathbb Z\cdot e(2)$ is concentrated 
in degree $1$ and $\mathrm A(1)$ in degree $0$. 
 
For $k\geqslant 3$, the cone exact sequence for $\mathrm{Cn}(k)$, 
\begin{multline*} 
\cdots\longrightarrow 
H^{m-1}\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k)\bigr)\xrightarrow{2\,\mathrm{St}^*\,} 
H^{m-1}\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k-1)\bigr)\longrightarrow H^m\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\bigr)\\ 
\longrightarrow 
H^{m}\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k)\bigr)\xrightarrow{2\,\mathrm{St}^*\,} 
H^{m}\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k-1)\bigr)\longrightarrow\cdots, 
\end{multline*} 
yields a short exact sequence 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow 
H^{m-1}\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k-1)\bigr)\big/\operatorname{\mathrm{Im}}(2\mathrm{St}^*) 
\longrightarrow 
H^m\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\bigr) 
\longrightarrow 
\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*) 
\longrightarrow 0. 
\] 
Since $\mathrm{St}^*$ is a surjection, we have 
$\operatorname{\mathrm{Im}}(2\mathrm{St}^*)=2H^{m-1}\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k-1)\bigr)$, 
and hence there is a short exact sequence 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow 
H^{m-1}\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k-1)\bigr)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2 
\longrightarrow 
H^m\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\bigr) 
\longrightarrow 
\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*) 
\longrightarrow 0. 
\] 
 
For $m=0,1$, the map 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}^*:H^m(\mathrm A(k)) 
\longrightarrow H^m(\mathrm A(k-1)) 
\] 
is an isomorphism between infinite cyclic groups, since 
$k\geqslant3$. Hence $\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)=0$ in these 
degrees, and the asserted formula follows from the short 
exact sequence above and Theorem~\ref{SeqS}. 
 
We may therefore assume that $m\geqslant2$. 
In this case, $H^m(\mathrm A(k))$ is finite, and the 
short exact sequence above consists of finite groups. 
 
For an abelian group $G$ and a prime $p$, denote by $G_{(p)}$ its $p$-primary component. 
The last exact sequence is a direct sum (over all primes $p$) of short exact sequences 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow \bigl(H^{m-1}(\mathrm{A}(k-1))\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2\bigr)_{(p)} 
\longrightarrow H^m\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\bigr)_{(p)} 
\xrightarrow{\ \theta\ } 
\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)_{(p)} 
\longrightarrow 0. 
\] 
For $p\neq 2$, the first term vanishes. 
We now show that for $p=2$, this short exact sequence splits; since Theorem~\ref{SeqS} implies that 
\[ 
\mathrm{Ker}\bigl(2\,\mathrm{St}^*:H^m(\mathrm{A}(k))\to H^m(\mathrm{A}(k-1))\bigr)\cong 
H^m\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(k)\bigr)\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits 
H^m\bigl(\mathrm{A}(k-1)\bigr)[2], 
\] 
establishing this splitting will complete the proof. 
 
By the splitting lemma for abelian groups (see \cite{Hatcher}, p.147), 
it suffices to construct a section of the map $\theta$; that is, a homomorphism 
\[ 
\eta:\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)_{(2)}\longrightarrow H^m\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\bigr)_{(2)} 
\] 
such that $\theta\circ\eta=\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)_{(2)}}$. 
 
The group $\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)_{(2)}$ is a 
squarefree-torsion $2$-group, so it can be viewed as a vector space over 
$\mathbb{F}_2$. Choose a basis $\{[a_i]\}_{i \in I}$ for 
$\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)_{(2)}$. For each basis element $[a_i]$, 
choose a cocycle representative $a_i\in\mathrm{A}^m(k)$. 
Consider the class $\mathrm{St}^*[a_i]\in H^m(\mathrm{A}(k-1))_{(2)}$. 
Since $2\,\mathrm{St}^*[a_i]=0$, there exists a cochain $b_i\in\mathrm{A}^{m-1}(k-1)$ 
with $\partial(b_i)=(-1)^m 2\,\mathrm{St}(a_i)$. 
For each basis element, set 
\[ 
u_i:=[(a_i,-b_i)]\in H^m(\mathrm{Cn}(k)). 
\] 
This yields a well-defined cohomology class for each basis element because 
\[ 
\partial(a_i,-b_i)=(\partial(a_i),(-1)^m 2\,\mathrm{St}(a_i)-\partial(b_i))=(0,0). 
\] 
It remains to verify that these lifts have order dividing $2$, 
so that the assignment extends to a homomorphism on 
$\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)_{(2)}$. 
Since $2[a_i]=0$, choose 
$c_i\in\mathrm A^{m-1}(k)$ with $\partial c_i=2a_i$. 
Set 
\[ 
v_i:=(-1)^m \mathrm{St}(c_i)-b_i. 
\] 
Then $\partial v_i=0$, and 
\[ 
2(a_i,-b_i)-\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}}(c_i,0)=(0,2v_i). 
\] 
Since $\mathrm{St}^*$ is surjective, the class $2[v_i]$ belongs to 
$\operatorname{Im}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)$ and hence maps to zero in 
$H^m(\mathrm{Cn}(k))$ by the cone exact sequence. 
Thus $2[(a_i,-b_i)]=0$. 
The assignment $[a_i]\mapsto[(a_i,-b_i)]$ therefore 
extends to a homomorphism 
\[ 
\eta:\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)_{(2)} 
\longrightarrow H^m(\mathrm{Cn}(k))_{(2)}. 
\] 
Since $\theta(\eta([a_i]))=[a_i]$ for every basis element, 
we have $\theta\circ\eta=\mathrm{id}$. 
Thus the short exact sequence splits, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corr-10: body_md -->
\label{HTn} 
For $n\geqslant 4$, the following isomorphism holds: 
\[ 
H^q(\mathrm T(n))\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\left[ 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant1} 
H^{q-2i}\bigl(\mathrm A_2(n-2i)\bigr) 
\right]&\\[2mm] 
\qquad\oplus 
\left[ 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant1} 
H^{q-2i-1}\bigl(\mathbf B_{n-2i-1}\bigr)\otimes\mathbb Z_2 
\right]&\\[2mm] 
\qquad\qquad\oplus 
\left[ 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant1} 
H^{q-2i}\bigl(\mathbf B_{n-2i-1}\bigr)[2] 
\right] 
&\text{if $q<n$},\\[4mm] 
\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n-1)\mathbb{Z}&\text{if $q=n$}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For $1\leqslant i<\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor$, Lemma~\ref{di} yields an isomorphism of complexes $\mathrm{T}_i(n)\cong\mathrm{Cn}(n-2i)$, 
where $\mathrm{T}^q_i(n)\cong\mathrm{Cn}^{q-2i}(n-2i)$, since 
\[ 
\mathrm{T}^q_i(n)= 
\mathrm{A}^{q-2i}(n-2i)\times y^{2i} 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits 
\mathrm{A}^{q-2i-1}(n-2i-1)\times y^{2i+1}. 
\] 
Therefore, Proposition~\ref{HTi00} implies that if $1\leqslant i<\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor$, then 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{T}_i(n)\bigr)\cong 
H^{q-2i}\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(n-2i)\bigr) 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits H^{q-2i-1}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1})\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1})[2]. 
\] 
Summing over $i$ and applying Corollary~\ref{Sum} completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{HDn00} 
For $n\geqslant 4$, the following isomorphism holds: 
\[ 
H^q(\mathbf{D}_n)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
H^q(\mathbf{B}_n)\oplus\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 0}H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i})\big/H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1})\\[2mm] 
\hspace{3.5em}\oplus\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 1}H^{q-2i-1}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1})\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2&\\[2mm] 
\hspace{6em}\oplus\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 1}H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1})[2]&\text{if $q<n$},\\[3mm] 
\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n-1)\mathbb{Z}&\text{if $q=n$}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{A2}, we know that 
\[ 
H^{q-2i}\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(n-2i)\bigr) 
\cong 
H^{q-2i}\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i}\bigr)\big/ H^{q-2i}\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1}\bigr). 
\] 
Therefore, Lemma~\ref{d0} and Corollaries~\ref{Sum} and \ref{HTn} give the declared isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{StabS_D} 
For $n\geqslant4$, there is a canonical morphism of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_D:\mathrm{D}(n)\longrightarrow\mathrm{D}(n-1) 
\] 
such that for any $q\geqslant 1$, the induced homomorphism 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}^*_D:H^q(\mathbf{D}_n)\longrightarrow H^q(\mathbf{D}_{n-1}) 
\] 
is an isomorphism if $n\geqslant 2q$. 
Thus, the cohomology of the family $\mathbf{D}$ stabilizes.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
For $n=4$, define $\mathrm{St}_D$ to be the canonical projection 
\[ 
\mathrm D(4)\cong 
\mathrm A(4)\oplus\mathrm A_2(4)\oplus\mathrm T(4) 
\longrightarrow \mathrm A(4)=\mathrm D(3). 
\] 
For $q=1,2$, Corollaries~\ref{A2} and~\ref{HTn} give 
$H^q(\mathrm A_2(4))=H^q(\mathrm T(4))=0$. 
Thus the assertion holds for $n=4$. 
Henceforth assume $n\geqslant5$. 
 
For $n\geqslant 5$, the target complex $\mathrm{D}(n-1)$ contains the subcomplex $\mathrm{T}(n-1)$. In this case, for elements of $\mathrm T(n)$, we set 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_D(c\times y^r)=\mathrm{St}(c)\times y^r, 
\qquad c\in \mathrm A(n-r). 
\] 
Lemma~\ref{di} implies that $\mathrm{St}_D:\mathrm T(n)\to\mathrm T(n-1)$ is a morphism of complexes. 
 
Using the canonical decomposition $\mathrm T_0(n)\cong \mathrm A(n)\oplus \mathrm A_2(n)$ from Lemma~\ref{d0}, we define 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_D(c_1\oplus c_2):=\mathrm{St}(c_1), 
\qquad c_1\in\mathrm{A}(n),\quad c_2\in\mathrm{A}_2(n). 
\] 
The right-hand side is taken in the $\mathrm{A}(n-1)$ 
summand of the canonical decomposition 
$\mathrm{T}_0(n-1)\cong\mathrm{A}(n-1)\oplus\mathrm{A}_2(n-1)$. 
Thus $\mathrm{St}_D$ is a morphism of complexes. 
 
It remains to prove that $\mathrm{St}^*_D$ induces isomorphisms on cohomology in the range $n\geqslant 2q$. 
 
\smallskip 
\noindent 
\textbf{1.} \emph{The subcomplex $\mathrm{T}(n)$.} 
For $1\leqslant i<\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, recall from the proof 
of Corollary~\ref{HTn} that we have an identification 
$\mathrm{T}_i^q(n)\cong\mathrm{Cn}^{q-2i}(n-2i)$, 
where $\mathrm{Cn}(n-2i)$ is the mapping cone of the chain map 
\[ 
2\,\mathrm{St}:\mathrm{A}(n-2i)\longrightarrow\mathrm{A}(n-2i-1). 
\] 
Under this identification, the chain map $\mathrm{St}_D$ acts on the cochain space 
\[ 
\mathrm{Cn}^m(n-2i)=\mathrm{A}^m(n-2i)\oplus\mathrm{A}^{m-1}(n-2i-1) 
\] 
by applying the operator $\mathrm{St}$ to both cochain factors simultaneously: 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{Cn}}(a, b) = \bigl(\mathrm{St}(a), \mathrm{St}(b)\bigr). 
\] 
Since $\mathrm{St}$ commutes with the differential $\partial$ 
and strictly satisfies $\mathrm{St}\circ(2\,\mathrm{St})=(2\,\mathrm{St})\circ\mathrm{St}$, 
the map $\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{Cn}}$ is a canonical morphism of mapping cones: 
\[ 
\begin{array}{ccc} 
\mathrm{A}(n-2i) & \xrightarrow{\;2\mathrm{St}\;} & \mathrm{A}(n-2i-1) \\ 
\Big\downarrow\rlap{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{St}$} & & \Big\downarrow\rlap{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{St}$} \\ 
\mathrm{A}(n-2i-1) & \xrightarrow{\;2\mathrm{St}\;} & \mathrm{A}(n-2i-2) 
\end{array} 
\] 
Put $m=q-2i$ and $k=n-2i$. 
Only indices with $2i\leqslant q$ need to be considered, 
since $\mathrm T_i(n)$ and $\mathrm T_i(n-1)$ have no 
cochains in degrees below $2i$. 
 
For $m\geqslant1$, the assumption $n\geqslant2q$ gives 
\[ 
k-1=n-2i-1\geqslant2m+2i-1\geqslant2m+1. 
\] 
Hence Theorem~\ref{StabSH} implies that both vertical maps 
in the diagram induce isomorphisms in degrees $m-1$ and $m$. 
For $m=0$, we have $k\geqslant3$; the maps in degree $0$ 
are the identity on $\mathbb Z$, and the groups in degree 
$-1$ vanish. 
 
The Five Lemma, applied to the induced diagram of long exact 
cohomology sequences, therefore gives an isomorphism 
\[ 
H^m(\mathrm{Cn}(k)) 
\longrightarrow H^m(\mathrm{Cn}(k-1)). 
\] 
Equivalently, 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_D^*:H^q(\mathrm T_i(n)) 
\longrightarrow H^q(\mathrm T_i(n-1)) 
\] 
is an isomorphism. Taking the direct sum over $i$ proves 
the assertion for $\mathrm T(n)$. 
 
\smallskip 
\noindent 
\textbf{2.} \emph{The subcomplex $\mathrm{T}_0(n)$.} 
By Lemma~\ref{d0}, we have $H^q(\mathrm{T}_0(n))\cong H^q(\mathrm{A}(n))\oplus H^q(\mathrm{A}_2(n))$. 
The map $\mathrm{St}_D^*$ acts as $\mathrm{St}^*$ on the first summand and is identically zero on the second. 
By Theorem~\ref{StabSH}, $\mathrm{St}^*:H^q(\mathrm{A}(n))\to H^q(\mathrm{A}(n-1))$ is an isomorphism for $n\geqslant 2q-1$.  
Furthermore, for $n\geqslant 2q$, Corollary~\ref{A2} shows that both $H^q(\mathrm{A}_2(n))=0$ and $H^q(\mathrm{A}_2(n-1))=0$. 
Thus, $\mathrm{St}_D^*:H^q(\mathrm{T}_0(n))\to H^q(\mathrm{T}_0(n-1))$ is an isomorphism for $n\geqslant 2q$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remnr-5: body_md -->
\label{StabS_D_Small} 
In order to define the stabilization morphisms for the affine 
families in subsequent sections across all dimensions, we will specify the chain map 
$\mathrm{St}_D:\mathrm{D}(m)\longrightarrow\mathrm{D}(m-1)$ 
for the cases $m \in \{1,2,3\}$.  
 
For these small values, we define $\mathrm{St}_D$ naturally  
as the algebraic restriction to the standard parabolic subgroup 
$D_{m-1}\subset D_m$ (where $D_0$ is the trivial group). 
Explicitly, on the basis elements of the Salvetti complex, 
$\mathrm{St}_D(P) = P$ if $P \subset D_{m-1}$, and $0$ otherwise. 
Because this restriction map inherently preserves the empty 
composition $P=\emptyset$, it induces the identity isomorphism on 
$H^0(\mathbf{D}_m)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ for all $m \geqslant 1$, 
which is the only homological property required from these  
low-dimensional components in the stable ranges.
<!-- end remnr-5 -->
<!-- corr-11: body_md -->
\label{StableD} 
The stable cohomology of the family $\mathbf{D}$ is given by the isomorphism: 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathbf{D}_\infty\bigr)\cong H^q(\mathbf{B}_\infty)\oplus 
\bigl[\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 1}H^{q-2i-1}(\mathbf{B}_\infty)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2\bigr]\oplus 
\bigl[\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 1}H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_\infty)[2]\bigr]. 
\] 
Thus, for any prime $p$, as well as for $p=0$, we have: 
\[ 
\mathrm{G}_p\bigl(\mathbf{D}_\infty;t\bigr)= 
\begin{cases} 
\mathrm{G}_p(\mathbf{B}_\infty;t)&\text{if $p\neq 2$},\\[1mm] 
\frac{1-t+t^2}{1-t}\;\mathrm{G}_2(\mathbf{B}_\infty;t)-\frac{t^2}{1-t}&\text{if $p=2$}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-11 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
If $n\geqslant 2q$, then by Theorem~\ref{StabSH} the quotient terms 
$H^{q-2i}(\mathbf B_{n-2i})/H^{q-2i}(\mathbf B_{n-2i-1})$ 
vanish for all $i\geqslant0$. Moreover, the stabilization maps identify 
\[ 
H^{q-2i-1}(\mathbf B_{n-2i-1}) 
\cong 
H^{q-2i-1}(\mathbf B_\infty)\qquad\text{and}\qquad H^{q-2i}(\mathbf B_{n-2i-1})[2] 
\cong 
H^{q-2i}(\mathbf B_\infty)[2] 
\] 
for all $i\geqslant1$ for which the corresponding summands are non-zero. 
Applying these identifications to Theorem~\ref{HDn00} gives the stated 
stable decomposition.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corr-12: body_md -->
\label{DQ} 
For $n\geqslant 4$, we have 
\[ 
\dim_{\mathbb{Q}} H^q\!\left(\mathbf{D}_n;\mathbb{Q}\right)= 
\begin{cases} 
1&\text{if $q=0,1$},\\ 
1&\text{if $q=n-1$ and $n$ is even},\\ 
1&\text{if $q=n$ and $n$ is even},\\ 
0&\text{otherwise.} 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
By Arnold's theorem (Corollary~\ref{Arn1}), $H^k(\mathbf{B}_m;\mathbb{Q})\cong\mathbb{Q}$ 
for $k\in\{0,1\}$ and $m \geqslant 2$, and vanishes for $k \geqslant 2$.  
Applying the functor $-\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ to the isomorphism in Theorem~\ref{HDn00} 
eliminates all $\mathbb{Z}_2$-torsion terms. 
 
For $q=n$, the term $\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n-1)\mathbb{Z}\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ 
yields $\mathbb{Q}$ if $n$ is even (since $\chi(n-1)=0$) and $0$ if $n$ is odd. 
For $q < n$, the base term $H^q(\mathbf{B}_n;\mathbb{Q})$ yields $\mathbb{Q}$ for $q=0, 1$.  
 
The remaining rational contribution comes from the quotient terms 
\[ 
H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i};\mathbb{Q}) \big/ H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1};\mathbb{Q}). 
\] 
For this quotient to be non-zero (i.e., isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}$), 
we must have $H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i};\mathbb{Q})\cong\mathbb{Q}$ 
and $H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1};\mathbb{Q})=0$. 
Since rational cohomology of braid groups is non-trivial only in dimensions 0 and 1, 
and the dimension 0 yields $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Q}=0$, we must strictly have $q-2i=1$.  
Furthermore, $H^1(\mathbf{B}_m;\mathbb{Q})$ vanishes only for $m < 2$. 
Thus, we need $n-2i \geqslant 2$ and $n-2i-1 < 2$, which uniquely forces $n-2i=2$. 
This relation implies $2i=n-2$, meaning $n$ must be even.  
Consequently, the degree is $q=1+2i=n-1$. In this case, exactly one quotient term survives, yielding $\mathbb{Q}$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- remnr-6: body_md -->
\label{RmGor} 
The integral cohomology of the groups $\mathbf D_n$ 
was previously studied by Goryunov~\cite{Gor}. 
Several entries in his table contain fewer cyclic 
summands of order $2$ than the corresponding groups 
given by Theorem~\ref{HDn00}. 
For example, our computations yield 
\[ 
H^7(\mathbf D_9)\cong(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^5, 
\qquad 
H^8(\mathbf D_{11})\cong(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^7, 
\] 
whereas Goryunov's table gives 
$(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^4$ and 
$(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^5$, respectively. 
For the ranks and degrees displayed in that table, 
the free parts and the odd-primary torsion agree 
with our results. 
 
The $2$-primary torsion is essential to the distinction 
between the stable cohomology of the family $\mathbf D$ 
and that of the braid groups 
(see Corollary~\ref{StableD}).
<!-- end remnr-6 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
\label{BStab} 
For $n\geqslant4$, there is an isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf B}_n\bigr) 
\cong 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{0\leqslant l\leqslant n-1} 
H^{q-l}\bigl(\mathbf D_{n-l-1}\bigr). 
\]
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
\label{StabS_B} 
For $n\geqslant 5$, there is a canonical morphism of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_{\widetilde B}:\widetilde{\mathrm B}(n) 
\longrightarrow 
\widetilde{\mathrm B}(n-1) 
\] 
such that the induced homomorphism 
$ 
\mathrm{St}_{\widetilde B}^*: 
H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf B}_n) 
\longrightarrow 
H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf B}_{n-1}) 
$\ 
is an isomorphism if $n\geqslant\max\{q+4,2q+1\}$.
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
On the summand $x^l\times\mathrm{D}(n-l-1)$, set 
$\mathrm{St}_{\widetilde B}(x^l\times c)=x^l\times \mathrm{St}_D(c)$. 
The last summand $x^{n-1}\times\mathrm{D}(0)$ is sent to zero. 
 
For a non-zero contribution to $H^q$, put 
$m=n-l-1$ and $d=q-l$. 
Under the stated assumptions, whenever $d>0$ we have $m\geqslant4$. 
Moreover, if $n\geqslant2q+1$, then 
\[ 
m=n-l-1\geqslant 2q-l\geqslant 2(q-l)=2d. 
\] 
If $d=0$, the assertion is clear. If $d>0$, then 
Theorem~\ref{StabS_D} implies that 
$H^d(\mathbf D_m)\longrightarrow H^d(\mathbf D_{m-1})$ 
is an isomorphism. Summing over $l$ gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corr-13: body_md -->
\label{StabB} 
For any $q\geqslant3$ and $n\geqslant2q$,\footnote{The shift by one in the stated stable range comes from applying 
Theorem~\ref{StabS_B} to the stabilization map at level $n+1$.} as well as for 
$q=2$ and $n\geqslant5$, the cohomology group 
$H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf B}_n)$ stabilizes. The stable cohomology is 
given by 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_\infty\bigr)\cong 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{m\geqslant 0}H^{q-m}\bigl(\mathbf{D}_\infty\bigr).  
\] 
Thus, for any prime $p$, as well as for $p=0$, we have: 
\begin{equation}\label{GB} 
\mathrm{G}_p\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_\infty;t\bigr)= 
\begin{cases} 
\frac{1}{1-t}\;\mathrm{G}_p(\mathbf{B}_\infty;t)&\text{if $p\neq 2$},\\[2mm] 
\frac{1-t+t^2}{(1-t)^2}\;\mathrm{G}_2(\mathbf{B}_\infty;t)-\frac{t^2}{(1-t)^2}&\text{if $p=2$}. 
\end{cases} 
\end{equation}
<!-- end corr-13 -->
<!-- corr-14: body_md -->
For $n\geqslant 4$, we have: 
\[ 
\dim_{\mathbb{Q}} H^q\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}_n;\mathbb{Q}\bigr)= 
\begin{cases} 
1&\text{if $q=0$},\\[1mm] 
2&\text{if $1\leqslant q<n-2$},\\[1mm] 
\left\lfloor\frac{n+3}{2}\right\rfloor&\text{if $q=n-2$ or $q=n-1$},\\ 
0&\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-14 -->
<!-- lmr-11: body_md -->
\label{D00} 
For $n\geqslant 5$, the action of $\partial_{\widetilde{D}}$ on 
$\overline{\mathrm{T}}(n-1)$ is determined by the commutation relation 
$\partial_{\widetilde{D}}\circ\overline{\sigma}=\overline{\sigma}\circ\partial_{\widetilde{D}}$ and the formula 
\[ 
\partial_{\widetilde{D}}(c)= 
\begin{cases} 
\partial_D(c)\mathbf{\dotplus}\overline{\sigma}\bigl(\partial_D(c)\bigr)&\text{if $c\in\mathrm{T}^{(1)}(n-1)$},\\ 
\partial_D(c)&\text{if $c\in\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)$}. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
In particular, $\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)$ is a subcomplex of\, $\overline{\mathrm{T}}(n-1)$.
<!-- end lmr-11 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
For $c\in\mathrm{T}^{(1)}(n-1)$ the formula follows from the definition of $\partial_{\widetilde{D}}$. 
 
For a basis cochain $c=(-1)^{\frac{a(a+1)}{2}}e(n_1,\dots,n_a)\times y^r\in\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)$ 
the definition of $\partial_{\widetilde{D}}$ yields: 
\[ 
\partial_{\widetilde{D}}(c)= 
\left.\frac{D_{n_1}(t)}{A_{n_1-1}(t)}\right|_{t=-1} 
e(n_2,\dots,n_a)\times y^r+\partial_D(c) 
=\partial_D(c). 
\] 
This proves the formula for $c\in\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lmr-12: body_md -->
\label{Dd0} 
For $n\geqslant 5$, there is a canonical isomorphism of complexes 
\[ 
\overline{\mathrm{T}}(n-1) 
\cong 
\mathrm{T}(n-1)\oplus\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1). 
\]
<!-- end lmr-12 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Define 
\[ 
\Delta\bigl(\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\bigr):=\{\,c+\overline{\sigma}(c)\mid c\in\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\,\}. 
\] 
Then 
\begin{multline*} 
\qquad\overline{\mathrm{T}}(n-1) 
=\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\oplus\mathrm{T}^{(1)}(n-1)\oplus\overline{\sigma}\bigl(\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\bigr)\\ 
=\mathrm{T}^{(1)}(n-1)\oplus\Delta\bigl(\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\bigr)\oplus\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1).\qquad 
\end{multline*} 
The formula for $\partial_{\widetilde{D}}$ given in Lemma~\ref{D00} 
shows that $\mathrm{T}^{(1)}(n-1)\oplus\Delta\bigl(\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\bigr)$ is a subcomplex of 
$\overline{\mathrm{T}}(n-1)$ isomorphic to $\mathrm{T}(n-1)$. 
Therefore, this decomposition of $\overline{\mathrm{T}}(n-1)$ yields the claimed isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lmr-13: body_md -->
\label{HTT} 
For $n\geqslant 5$, there is an isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\bigr)\cong\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{r\geqslant 2} H^{q-r}\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(n-r-1)\bigr). 
\]
<!-- end lmr-13 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
For every $r\geqslant2$, put $m=n-r-1$ and consider the column 
\[ 
C_r:=\overline{\mathrm A}_2(m)\times y^r 
\] 
with the part of the differential which preserves the exponent of 
$y$. This column complex is just the complex 
$\overline{\mathrm A}_2(m)$, shifted in degree by $r$. 
 
Define 
\[ 
\Phi_r:C_r\longrightarrow \mathrm A_2(m)\times y^r\qquad\text{by} 
\qquad 
\Phi_r(c\times y^r):=\tau(c)\times y^r . 
\] 
Since 
\[ 
\overline{\mathrm A}_2(m)= 
\mathrm{Ker}\bigl(\overline{\mathrm{St}}:\mathrm{A}(m)\to\mathrm{A}(m-1)\bigr), 
\qquad 
\overline{\mathrm{St}}=\tau\mathrm{St}\tau , 
\] 
we have 
$\overline{\mathrm{St}}(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{St}(\tau c)=0$. 
Thus $\Phi_r$ maps $C_r$ isomorphically onto 
$\mathrm A_2(m)\times y^r$. Since $\tau$ commutes with the 
differential of $\mathrm A(m)$, $\Phi_r$ is an isomorphism of 
column complexes. Hence 
\[ 
H^q(C_r) 
\cong 
H^{q-r}\bigl(\mathrm A_2(n-r-1)\bigr). 
\] 
 
It remains to take into account the part of the total differential 
which changes the exponent of $y$. This part contains the factor 
$\chi(r)$, and therefore it is zero for odd $r$. Hence 
$\mathrm T^{(2)}(n-1)$ decomposes into the direct sum, over 
$a\geqslant1$, of two-column complexes 
\[ 
K_a:\quad 
C_{2a}\longrightarrow C_{2a+1}. 
\] 
Here 
\[ 
C_{2a}=\overline{\mathrm A}_2(n-2a-1)\times y^{2a}, 
\qquad 
C_{2a+1}=\overline{\mathrm A}_2(n-2a-2)\times y^{2a+1}. 
\] 
 
Since the weights $n-2a-1$ and $n-2a-2$ have opposite parities, and 
$H^*(\mathrm A_2(k))=0$ for odd $k$, one of the two column 
complexes $C_{2a}$, $C_{2a+1}$ is acyclic. Therefore the short exact 
sequence 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow C_{2a+1}\longrightarrow K_a\longrightarrow C_{2a} 
\longrightarrow0 
\] 
gives, by the associated long exact cohomology sequence, 
\[ 
H^q(K_a) 
\cong 
H^q(C_{2a})\oplus H^q(C_{2a+1}). 
\] 
This is canonical, because one of the two summands is zero. 
 
Taking the direct sum over all $a\geqslant1$, we obtain the required isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lmr-14: body_md -->
\label{HDDT0} 
For $n\geqslant 5$, the following isomorphism holds: 
\begin{multline*} 
\qquad H^q\bigl(\overline{\mathrm T}_0(n-1)\bigr) 
\cong 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm T_0(n-1)\bigr) 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm A_2(n-1)\bigr)\\ 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits 
\frac{\chi(n-1)}{2}\, 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm A_2(n-1)\bigr) 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits 
\frac{\chi(n)}{2}\, 
H^{q-1}\bigl(\mathrm A_2(n-2)\bigr).\qquad 
\end{multline*}
<!-- end lmr-14 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Similarly to Lemma~\ref{Dd0}, we obtain a canonical isomorphism of complexes 
\[ 
\overline{\mathrm{T}}_0(n-1)\cong\mathrm{T}_0(n-1)\oplus\mathrm{T}^{(0)}_0(n-1), 
\qquad\text{where}\qquad 
\mathrm{T}^{(0)}_0(n-1):=\overline{\mathrm{A}}_2(n-1)+\sigma\bigl(\overline{\mathrm{A}}_2(n-1)\bigr) 
\] 
and, similarly to Lemma~\ref{d0}, we obtain a canonical isomorphism of complexes 
\[
