\mathrm{T}^{(0)}_0(n-1)\cong\overline{\mathrm{A}}_2(n-1)\oplus\mathrm{A}_{2,2}(n-1), 
\] 
where $\mathrm{A}_{2,2}(n-1)=\mathrm{Ker}(\mathrm{St})\cap\mathrm{Ker}(\overline{\mathrm{St}})$. 
 
It remains to compute $H^*(\mathrm{A}_{2,2}(n-1))$. 
The morphism of complexes $\overline{\mathrm{St}}:\mathrm{A}_2(m)\to\mathrm{A}_2(m-1)$ 
is surjective and induces a short exact sequence of complexes 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow \mathrm{A}_{2,2}(m) 
\longrightarrow \mathrm{A}_2(m)\xrightarrow{\;\overline{\mathrm{St}}\;}\mathrm{A}_2(m-1)\longrightarrow 0. 
\] 
This yields a long exact sequence in cohomology. 
Since $H^*(\mathrm{A}_2(k))$ vanishes when $k$ is odd, this sequence 
shows that 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}_{2,2}(m)\bigr)\cong 
\begin{cases}  
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(m)\bigr)&\text{if $m$ is even},\\ 
H^{q-1}\bigl(\mathrm{A}_2(m-1)\bigr)&\text{if $m$ is odd}. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
This isomorphism, for $m=n-1$, implies the isomorphism of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-23: body_md -->
\label{HK1} 
For $n\geqslant 5$, the following isomorphism holds: 
 
If $q<n-1$, then 
\begin{align*} 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm{K}_1(n)\bigr) &\cong H^q\bigl(\mathbf{D}_{n-1}\bigr)\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits 
\bigl[H^q(\mathbf{B}_{n-1})\big/H^q(\mathbf{B}_{n-2})\bigl] 
\\[2mm] 
&\hspace{2em}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits\frac{\chi(n-1)}{2}H^q(\mathbf{B}_{n-1})\big/H^q(\mathbf{B}_{n-2}) 
\\[2mm] 
&\hspace{2em}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits\frac{\chi(n)}{2}H^{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2})\big/H^{q-1}(\mathbf{B}_{n-3}) 
\\[2mm] 
&\hspace{2em}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 1}\bigl[H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-1})\big/H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-2})\bigr] 
\\[2mm] 
&\hspace{2em}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 1} \bigl[H^{q-2i-1}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-2})\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2 
\oplus H^{q-2i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-2i-2})[2]\bigr] 
\\[2mm] 
&\hspace{2em}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 2} 
\bigl[H^{q-i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-i-1})\big/H^{q-i}(\mathbf{B}_{n-i-2})\bigr]^{\oplus 2}. 
\\[4mm] 
H^{n-1}\bigl(\mathrm{K}_1(n)\bigr)&\cong\mathbb{Z}^{\oplus 2}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits\bigl[\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n)\mathbb{Z}\bigr]^{\oplus 2}. 
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-23 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
From the isomorphism~\eqref{K}, we assemble the cohomology $H^q\bigl(\mathrm{K}_1(n)\bigr)$ 
by summing the components of $\overline{\mathrm{T}}_0(n-1)$ and $\bigl[\overline{\mathrm{T}}(n-1)\bigr]^{\oplus 2}$ 
obtained in Lemmas~\ref{Dd0}, \ref{HTT}, and \ref{HDDT0}. 
The base terms $\mathrm{T}_0(n-1)$ and one copy of $\mathrm{T}(n-1)$ 
exactly reconstruct the cohomology of the group $\mathbf{D}_{n-1}$ 
via the decomposition~\eqref{DecD}.  
 
For $q < n-1$, the explicit sums in the theorem correspond directly to the remaining components.  
Applying Corollary~\ref{HTn} to the second copy of $\mathrm{T}(n-1)$ yields the sums over $i \geqslant 1$. 
The residual terms from $\overline{\mathrm{T}}_0(n-1)$ (Lemma~\ref{HDDT0}) 
give the terms involving $\mathrm A_2(n-1)$ and $\mathrm A_2(n-2)$. 
Finally, Lemma~\ref{HTT} applied to the doubled complex 
$\bigl[\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\bigr]^{\oplus 2}$ yields the last sum  
$\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 2} H^{q-i}\bigl(\mathrm A_2(n-i-1)\bigr)^{\oplus 2}$ (substituting $r=i$). 
 
At the top degree $q=n-1$, we evaluate each of these components using Corollary~\ref{A2}.  
Since $H^m(\mathrm A_2(m))\cong H^{(m)}_0(\Gamma[z])$, it is non-zero only for $m=0$, where $H^0(\mathrm A_2(0))\cong\mathbb{Z}$. 
\begin{itemize} 
    \item[--] The base $H^{n-1}(\mathbf{D}_{n-1})$ contributes $\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n)\mathbb{Z}$. 
    \item[--] By Corollary~\ref{HTn}, the second copy of $H^{n-1}(\mathrm{T}(n-1))$ 
    also contributes exactly $\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n)\mathbb{Z}$. 
    \item[--] In the residual part of $\overline{\mathrm{T}}_0(n-1)$, 
    the terms $H^{n-1}(\mathrm A_2(n-1))$ and $H^{n-2}(\mathrm A_2(n-2))$ 
    vanish because $n \geqslant 5$ (thus $n-1>0$ and $n-2>0$). 
    \item[--] The doubled complex $\bigl[\mathrm{T}^{(2)}(n-1)\bigr]^{\oplus 2}$ 
    contributes $\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{r\geqslant 2} H^{n-1-r}(\mathrm{A}_2(n-r-1))^{\oplus 2}$. 
    Letting $m=n-r-1$, we see this is non-zero only when $m=0$, which implies $r=n-1$. 
    Since $n \geqslant 5$, the index $r=n-1 \geqslant 4\geqslant 2$ is included in the sum. 
    This term yields $H^0(\mathrm{A}_2(0))^{\oplus 2}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{\oplus 2}$. 
\end{itemize} 
Summing these non-vanishing contributions gives exactly 
$\mathbb{Z}^{\oplus 2}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits\bigl[\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n)\mathbb{Z}\bigr]^{\oplus 2}$, 
completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lmr-15: body_md -->
\label{LmD2Zero} 
The spectral sequence associated with the filtration $F_p(n)$ 
of $\mathrm K_2(n)$ collapses at $E_2$.
<!-- end lmr-15 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The block decomposition implies that $d_r=0$ for 
$r\geqslant3$. Within each block, the only potentially 
nonzero $d_2$ goes from its even-even corner to its 
odd-odd corner. 
 
Fix a block and put $m=n-2a-2b-1$. 
If $m<2$, its odd-odd corner is zero. 
For $m\geqslant2$, surjectivity of $\mathrm{St}^*$ identifies the target 
of this potential differential with 
\[ 
E_2^{2a+2b+2,j-1}\big|_{\mathrm{block}} 
\cong 
H^{j-1}\bigl(\mathrm A(m-2)\bigr) 
\big/ 
2H^{j-1}\bigl(\mathrm A(m-2)\bigr). 
\] 
In particular, this target is annihilated by $2$. 
 
Suppose first that $j\geqslant3$. 
The source is a subgroup of the finite squarefree-torsion 
group $H^j(\mathrm A(m))$. 
Its odd-primary components map trivially to the target, 
so it remains to consider its $2$-primary component. 
Represent a class in this component by 
\[ 
u=x^{2a}\times c\times y^{2b}, 
\qquad \partial c=0. 
\] 
Since $2[c]=0$, choose $w\in\mathrm A^{j-1}(m)$ with 
$\partial w=2c$, and set 
\[ 
t=x^{2a}\times w\times y^{2b}. 
\] 
Write the total differential as 
\[ 
\partial_{\widetilde D}=d_v+2h, 
\] 
where $d_v$ preserves the filtration degree and $h$ raises 
it by one. The identity $\partial_{\widetilde D}^{\,2}=0$, 
together with freeness of the cochain groups, gives 
\[ 
d_vh+hd_v=0,\qquad h^2=0. 
\] 
Since $d_vt=2u$, the cochain $v=ht$ satisfies 
\[ 
d_vv=-h(d_vt)=-2hu, 
\qquad 
2hv=2h^2t=0. 
\] 
Thus $u+v$ is a total cocycle lifting $u$, and $d_2[u]=0$. 
 
It remains to consider $j\leqslant2$. 
For $j=0$, the target has negative cohomological degree 
and is zero. For $j=2$, the source is zero because 
$H^2(\mathrm A(m))=0$. 
For $j=1$, the source at the even-even corner vanishes 
unless $m=2$: for $m\geqslant3$, the map 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}^*:H^1(\mathrm A(m))\longrightarrow 
H^1(\mathrm A(m-1)) 
\] 
is an isomorphism between infinite cyclic groups. 
When $m=2$, the source is generated by $[e(2)]$. 
Both $\mathrm{St}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{St}}$ annihilate $e(2)$, so this 
generator is already represented by a total cocycle. 
Hence $d_2=0$ also in this case. 
Therefore all differentials $d_r$, $r\geqslant2$, vanish.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lmr-16: body_md -->
\label{LmExH} 
For $m=n-2a-2b-1$, the complex \eqref{3Complex} is isomorphic to the complex 
\begin{equation}\label{ExH} 
0\longrightarrow H^j\bigl(\mathbf{B}_m\bigr) 
\xrightarrow{(2\,\mathrm{St}^*,2\,\mathrm{St}^*)} H^j\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{m-1}\bigr)^{\oplus 2} 
\xrightarrow{(2\,\mathrm{St}^*,-2\,\mathrm{St}^*)} H^j\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{m-2}\bigr) 
\longrightarrow 0. 
\end{equation}
<!-- end lmr-16 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The components of the complex \eqref{3Complex} naturally form a  
$2\times 2$ bicomplex corresponding to the coordinates $(l,r)\in\{2a,2a+1\}\times\{2b, 2b+1\}$. 
The complex \eqref{3Complex} is exactly the total complex of this bicomplex. 
 
These terms are canonically identified with the cohomology groups 
$H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)$, $H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\oplus H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})$, and $H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-2})$. 
Evaluating the differential $d_1$ (whose explicit formula is given right after \eqref{SE1}) 
on these components yields the boundary maps. 
For the first map, the source has even indices $l=2a$ and $r=2b$, 
so $\chi(l)=\chi(r)=2$. The differential maps a class $u \in H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)$ to: 
\[ 
u\mapsto\bigl(2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*(u),\,2(-1)^{2a+j}\,\mathrm{St}^*(u)\bigr) 
=\bigl(2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*(u),\,2(-1)^j\,\mathrm{St}^*(u)\bigr). 
\] 
For the second map, the source components have indices $(2a+1,2b)$ and $(2a,2b+1)$. 
Since $\chi(\text{odd})=0$, one term in the differential vanishes in each case. 
A pair $(v_1,v_2)$ from the direct sum maps to the final term as: 
\[ 
(v_1,v_2)\mapsto 2(-1)^{2a+1+j}\,\mathrm{St}^*(v_1)+2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*(v_2)= 
-2(-1)^j\,\mathrm{St}^*(v_1)+ 2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*(v_2). 
\] 
 
We make two changes of coordinates. First, we change coordinates in the second direct summand 
by setting $v_2=(-1)^j v_2'$. In these coordinates, 
the first map becomes 
\[ 
u\mapsto\bigl(2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*(u), 
2\,\mathrm{St}^*(u)\bigr), 
\] 
and the second becomes 
\[ 
(v_1,v_2')\mapsto 
-2(-1)^j\,\mathrm{St}^*(v_1) 
+2(-1)^j\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*(v_2'). 
\] 
Second, we change coordinates in the final term 
$H^j(\mathbf B_{m-2})$ by multiplication by 
$(-1)^{j+1}$. The second map then takes the form 
\[ 
(v_1,v_2')\mapsto 
2\,\mathrm{St}^*(v_1)-2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*(v_2'). 
\] 
We next verify that $\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*=\mathrm{St}^*$. 
With the orientation signs induced by reversal of the 
ordered vertices, the operator $\overline{\mathrm{St}}=\tau \mathrm{St}\tau$ 
acts on the Fuchs basis in cohomological degree $j$ by 
\[ 
\overline{\mathrm{St}}\,e(n_1,\ldots,n_a)= 
\begin{cases} 
(-1)^j e(n_2,\ldots,n_a),&n_1=1,\\ 
0,&n_1>1. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
By the proof of Theorem~\ref{SeqS}, every cohomology 
class is a sum of classes represented by shuffle cycles 
$c*e(1_k)$, where 
$c\in C_{2r-j}^{(2r)}(\Gamma[z])$ is a cycle 
and $k=m-2r$. 
For $k\geqslant1$, the shuffle terms beginning with 
$e(1)$ acquire the sign $(-1)^{2r-j}=(-1)^j$ 
when this initial letter is removed. 
This sign cancels the sign in the formula for 
$\overline{\mathrm{St}}$. Consequently, 
\[ 
\overline{\mathrm{St}}(c*e(1_k))=\mathrm{St}(c*e(1_k))=c*e(1_{k-1}). 
\] 
For $k=0$, both operators vanish, since every letter 
of $c$ has positive even weight. 
Thus $\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*=\mathrm{St}^*$, and substituting 
$\mathrm{St}^*$ for $\overline{\mathrm{St}}^*$ in the maps 
yields exactly the complex \eqref{ExH}. 
Here terms with a negative braid index are understood to be zero.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lmr-17: body_md -->
\label{LmH} 
There are the following isomorphisms: 
\begin{equation}\label{H01} 
\mathrm{H}^{[0]}(m)= 
\begin{cases} 
\{\mathbb{Z},0,0\}&\text{if $m=0$},\\ 
\{0,\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2,0\}&\text{if $m=1$},\\ 
\{0,\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}_2\}&\text{if $m\geqslant 2$}, 
\end{cases} 
\qquad 
\mathrm{H}^{[1]}(m)= 
\begin{cases} 
\{0,0,0\}&\text{if $m=0,1$},\\ 
\{\mathbb{Z},0,0\}&\text{if $m=2$},\\ 
\{0,\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2,0\}&\text{if $m=3$},\\ 
\{0,\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}_2\}&\text{if $m\geqslant 4$}, 
\end{cases} 
\end{equation} 
\begin{equation}\label{H2} 
\mathrm{H}^{[2]}(m)=\{0,0,0\}. 
\end{equation} 
Furthermore, for $j\geqslant 3$, there are the following isomorphisms: 
\begin{equation}\label{Hq3} 
\begin{aligned} 
\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_0(m)&\cong\bigl[H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)\big/H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\bigr] 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2, 
\\ 
\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_1(m)&\cong\bigl[H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\big/H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-2})\bigr] 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-2})\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2, 
\\ 
\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_2(m)&\cong H^j\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{m-2}\bigr)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2. 
\end{aligned} 
\end{equation}
<!-- end lmr-17 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The isomorphisms \eqref{H01} easily follow from Theorem~\ref{SeqS} and the isomorphisms 
\[ 
H^0(\mathbf{B}_m)\cong\mathbb{Z}\;\;\text{if $m\geqslant 0$},\quad 
H^1(\mathbf{B}_m)\cong 
\begin{cases} 
\mathbb{Z}&\text{if $m\geqslant 2$},\\ 
0&\text{if $m\leqslant 1$}, 
\end{cases} 
\quad 
H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)\cong 0\;\;\text{if $m\leqslant 2$ and $j\geqslant 2$}, 
\] 
together with the fact that the homology groups of the $3$-term complex 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow\mathbb{Z} 
\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad 
\text{where\quad $\alpha(a)=(2a,2a),\,\beta(a,b)=2a-2b$}, 
\] 
are $\{0,\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}_2\}$. 
 
The identity \eqref{H2} follows from the vanishing of 
$H^2(\mathbf{B}_m)$ for all $m\geqslant 0$, which forces the complex \eqref{ExH} to be trivial. 
 
It remains to justify the formulas \eqref{Hq3} for $j\geqslant 3$. 
If $j\geqslant m$, all groups involved in \eqref{Hq3} vanish for 
degree reasons. Therefore we may assume $3\leqslant j<m$. 
 
Since the groups $H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)$ are finite, 
using Theorem~\ref{SeqS} and Corollary~\ref{A2}, we obtain a split exact sequence 
of finite groups: 
\[ 
0\longrightarrow H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)\big/H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1}) 
\longrightarrow H^j\bigl(\mathbf{B}_m\bigr) 
\stackrel{\mathrm{St}^*}\longrightarrow H^j\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{m-1}\bigr) 
\longrightarrow 0,\qquad 3\leqslant j<m. 
\] 
Since $\mathrm{St}^*$ is a surjection, we have: 
\begin{eqnarray*} 
\mathrm{Ker}\bigl(2\,\mathrm{St}^*:H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)\longrightarrow H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\bigr)&\cong& 
 H^j(\mathbf{B}_m)\big/H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits 
H^j\bigl(\mathbf{B}_{m-1}\bigr)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_2,\\ 
\mathrm{Im}\bigl(2\,\mathrm{St}^*:H^j(\mathbf{B}_m) 
\longrightarrow H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\bigr) 
&\cong& 2\,H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1}). 
\end{eqnarray*} 
These isomorphisms evaluated on the complex~\eqref{ExH} directly yield 
$\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_0(m)$ and $\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_2(m)$, which are naturally isomorphic to 
$\mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)$ and $\mathrm{Coker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)$, respectively.  
For the middle homology $\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_1(m)$, the kernel of the map $(2\,\mathrm{St}^*, -2\,\mathrm{St}^*)$ 
consists of pairs $(x,y)$ such that $x-y\in \mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)$, giving an isomorphism 
with $H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\oplus \mathrm{Ker}(2\,\mathrm{St}^*)$.  
The image of $(2\,\mathrm{St}^*, 2\,\mathrm{St}^*)$ is the diagonal subgroup consisting of elements 
$(2w,2w)$ where $w\in H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})$.  
Taking the quotient yields 
\[ 
\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_1(m)\cong\bigl[H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\big/2H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\bigr] 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\limits\mathrm{Ker}\bigl(2\,\mathrm{St}^*:H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-1})\to H^j(\mathbf{B}_{m-2})\bigr), 
\] 
which precisely expands to the three summands in $\mathrm{H}^{[j]}_1(m)$ via the established isomorphisms.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- theorem-24: body_md -->
\label{HK2} 
For $n\geqslant5$, one has $H^q(\mathrm K_2(n))=0$ for 
$q\leqslant 3$. For $q\geqslant 4$, there is an isomorphism 
\[ 
H^q\bigl(\mathrm K_2(n)\bigr) 
\cong 
\bigoplus_{\substack{p\ {\rm even},\ 4\leqslant p\leqslant n-1\\ 
j+p=q}} 
\mathcal D^j(n-p-1)^{\oplus(p/2-1)} . 
\]
<!-- end theorem-24 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Since $\mathrm K_2(n)$ has no cochains in degrees below $4$, 
we have $H^q(\mathrm K_2(n))=0$ for $q\leqslant3$. 
Lemmas~\ref{LmD2Zero} and~\ref{LmH} determine 
$E_\infty(n)=E_2(n)$ and hence all successive quotients of the induced 
filtration on $H^q(\mathrm K_2(n))$. To obtain the asserted direct sum 
decomposition of the cohomology itself, it remains to prove that this 
filtration splits over $\mathbb Z$. 
 
The block decomposition of the spectral sequence comes from a direct sum 
decomposition of the filtered cochain complex $\mathrm K_2(n)$ itself. 
Each block supported at 
\[ 
(2a,2b),\quad(2a+1,2b),\quad(2a,2b+1),\quad(2a+1,2b+1) 
\] 
is preserved by the total differential $\partial_{\widetilde D}$. 
Consequently, the cohomology is the direct sum of the cohomology groups of 
these blocks. The remaining extension problem therefore concerns the 
filtration within each individual block. 
 
Let $X$ be one such block with lower-left corner $(2a, 2b)$. 
The elements of $X$ carry the common factor $x^{2a}\times\cdots\times y^{2b}$, 
shifting the cohomological degree by $p_0=2a+2b$. 
Let $Y$ be the underlying unshifted complex, so that $X\cong Y[-p_0]$ and $H^q(X)\cong H^{q-p_0}(Y)$. 
Setting $j=q-p_0$ and $m=n-p_0-1$, the complex $Y$ is the total complex of the anti-commutative square (bicomplex): 
\[ 
\begin{array}{ccc} 
\mathrm{A}(m) & \xrightarrow{2\,\mathrm{St}} & \mathrm{A}(m-1) \\ 
2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}\downarrow \phantom{2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}} & 
& \phantom{-2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}} \downarrow -2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}} \\ 
\mathrm{A}(m-1) & \xrightarrow{2\,\mathrm{St}} & \mathrm{A}(m-2) 
\end{array} 
\] 
Thus, $Y$ can be viewed as the mapping cone of the chain map 
$2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}:\mathrm{Cn}(m)\to\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)$, 
where $\mathrm{Cn}(k)=\mathrm{Cone}\bigl(2\,\mathrm{St}:\mathrm{A}(k)\to\mathrm{A}(k-1)\bigr)$ 
is the complex studied in Proposition~\ref{HTi00}. 
 
It remains to show that the induced filtration on 
$H^j(Y)$ splits over $\mathbb Z$, yielding 
$H^j(Y)\cong\mathcal D^j(m)$. 
 
First, consider an odd prime $\ell$. 
Since multiplication by $2$ is an automorphism over $\mathbb{Z}_{(\ell)}$, 
Theorem~\ref{SeqS} and the complex \eqref{ExH} give: 
\[ 
H_0^{[s]}(m)_{(\ell)}\cong H^s(\mathrm A_2(m))_{(\ell)},\qquad 
H_1^{[s]}(m)_{(\ell)}\cong H^s(\mathrm A_2(m-1))_{(\ell)},\qquad 
H_2^{[s]}(m)_{(\ell)}=0. 
\] 
Since $H^*(\mathrm A_2(k))=0$ for odd $k$, the $\ell$-primary part of the 
$E_\infty$-page of each block is concentrated in at most one filtration degree 
(because $m$ and $m-1$ have opposite parities). Hence, there are absolutely 
no extension problems for odd-primary components. 
 
To analyze the $2$-primary extensions, we localize the complexes at the prime 
$2$ by tensoring with $\mathbb{Z}_{(2)}$, and analyze two cases based on $m$. 
For a complex $Z$, write 
$Z_{(2)}:=Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z_{(2)}$. 
 
\emph{Case 1: $m \geqslant 4$.} 
For $k\geqslant3$, the cone exact sequence gives 
\[ 
H^0(\mathrm{Cn}(k))=0,\qquad 
H^1(\mathrm{Cn}(k))\cong H^2(\mathrm{Cn}(k)) 
\cong\mathbb Z_2. 
\] 
Together with Proposition~\ref{HTi00}, this shows that 
\[ 
2\,H^i\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\otimes\mathbb Z_{(2)}\bigr)=0 
\qquad\text{for every }i. 
\] 
Since $m\geqslant4$, this applies to both 
$\mathrm{Cn}(m)$ and $\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)$. 
 
Let $(u,v)\in Y_{(2)}$ be a cocycle of degree $j$. 
The differential in the cone $Y=\mathrm{Cone}(2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}})$ 
is given by 
$\partial_Y(u,v)=\bigl(\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m)} u,\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)}v+(-1)^j\,2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}(u)\bigr)$. 
Since $u$ is a cycle in $\mathrm{Cn}(m)_{(2)}$ and its cohomology 
group is a squarefree-torsion $2$-group, there exists a cochain 
$w\in\mathrm{Cn}^{j-1}(m)_{(2)}$ such that $2u=\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m)} w$.  
Evaluating the boundary of $(w,0)$, we get $\partial_Y(w,0)=\bigl(2u,(-1)^{j-1}\,2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}(w)\bigr)$.  
Subtracting this from $2(u,v)$ yields: 
\[ 
2(u,v)-\partial_Y(w,0) 
=\bigl(0,2v+(-1)^j\,2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}(w)\bigr) 
=(0,2z). 
\] 
Set $z=v+(-1)^j\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}(w)\in\mathrm{Cn}^{j-1}(m-1)_{(2)}$. 
The cocycle condition for $(u,v)$ implies $\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)}v+(-1)^j\,2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}(u)=0$. Therefore,  
\[ 
\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)}z=\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)}v+(-1)^j\,\overline{\mathrm{St}} 
(\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m)}w)=\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)}v+(-1)^j\,2\,\overline{\mathrm{St}}(u)=0, 
\] 
showing that $z$ is a cycle in $\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)_{(2)}$. 
Since $H^{j-1}(\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)_{(2)})$ is a squarefree-torsion $2$-group, 
there exists $t$ such that $2z=\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)} t$. 
This gives $2[(u,v)]=[(0,2z)]=[(0,\partial_{\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)}t)]=0$. 
Thus $H^j(Y_{(2)})$ is annihilated by $2$. 
Its filtration is therefore a filtration of 
$\mathbb F_2$-vector spaces and splits. 
 
\emph{Case 2: $0\leqslant m\leqslant3$.} 
In this case, 
\[ 
Y^j=\mathrm A^j(m)\oplus 
\mathrm A^{j-1}(m-1)^{\oplus2}\oplus 
\mathrm A^{j-2}(m-2)=0 
\qquad(j\geqslant3). 
\] 
For $m=0$, the complex consists of $\mathbb Z$ in degree $0$. 
For $m=1$, it is 
$\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{(2,2)}\mathbb Z^2$. 
For $m=2$, it is 
$\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{(0,2,2)}\mathbb Z^3\xrightarrow{(0,-2,2)}\mathbb{Z}, 
$ 
with the leftmost term in degree $0$. 
 
The subscripts $L$, $R$, and $LR$ indicate the copies 
of the Fuchs complexes at the corners 
$(2a+1,2b)$, $(2a,2b+1)$, and $(2a+1,2b+1)$, 
respectively; elements without subscripts belong 
to the corner $(2a,2b)$. 
For $m=3$, choose the ordered bases 
\begin{gather*} 
Y^0:=e(1,1,1),\qquad Y^1:=\bigl\{e(1,2),\,e(2,1),\,e(1,1)_L,\,e(1,1)_R\bigr\},\\ 
Y^2:=\bigl\{e(3),\,e(2)_L,\,e(2)_R,\,e(1)_{LR}\bigr\}. 
\end{gather*} 
The differential matrices are 
\[ 
d^0= 
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}, 
\qquad 
d^1= 
\begin{pmatrix} 
-1&-1&0&0\\ 
-2&0&0&0\\ 
0&-2&0&0\\ 
0&0&-2&2 
\end{pmatrix}. 
\] 
These complexes give 
\[ 
\begin{array}{c|ccc} 
m&H^0(Y)&H^1(Y)&H^2(Y)\\ \hline 
0&\mathbb{Z}&0&0\\ 
1&0&\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2&0\\ 
2&0&\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb Z_2&\mathbb{Z}_2\\ 
3&0&\mathbb{Z}_2&\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2^{\oplus2}. 
\end{array} 
\] 
Comparison with Lemma~\ref{LmH} yields 
$H^j(Y)\cong\mathcal D^j(m)$ in every case. 
 
In all cases, all extensions split, yielding $H^q(X)\cong H^{q-p_0}(Y)\cong\mathcal{D}^j(m)$.  
Since for a fixed even $p_0=p\geqslant 4$ there are exactly 
$\frac{p}{2}-1$ isolated blocks summing to $p$, 
each block $\mathcal{D}^j(n-p-1)$ appears with this exact multiplicity.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
For $k\geqslant3$, the cone exact sequence gives 
\[ 
H^0(\mathrm{Cn}(k))=0,\qquad 
H^1(\mathrm{Cn}(k))\cong H^2(\mathrm{Cn}(k)) 
\cong\mathbb Z_2. 
\] 
Together with Proposition~\ref{HTi00}, this shows that 
\[ 
2\,H^i\bigl(\mathrm{Cn}(k)\otimes\mathbb Z_{(2)}\bigr)=0 
\qquad\text{for every }i. 
\] 
Since $m\geqslant4$, this applies to both 
$\mathrm{Cn}(m)$ and $\mathrm{Cn}(m-1)$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
In this case, 
\[ 
Y^j=\mathrm A^j(m)\oplus 
\mathrm A^{j-1}(m-1)^{\oplus2}\oplus 
\mathrm A^{j-2}(m-2)=0 
\qquad(j\geqslant3). 
\] 
For $m=0$, the complex consists of $\mathbb Z$ in degree $0$. 
For $m=1$, it is 
$\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{(2,2)}\mathbb Z^2$. 
For $m=2$, it is 
$\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{(0,2,2)}\mathbb Z^3\xrightarrow{(0,-2,2)}\mathbb{Z}, 
$ 
with the leftmost term in degree $0$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- theorem-25: body_md -->
\label{StabS_DD} 
For $n\geqslant6$, there is a canonical morphism of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_{\widetilde D}:\widetilde{\mathrm{D}}(n) 
\longrightarrow 
\widetilde{\mathrm{D}}(n-1). 
\] 
For any $q\geqslant1$, the induced homomorphism 
$ 
\mathrm{St}^*_{\widetilde D}: 
H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf D}_n) 
\longrightarrow 
H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf D}_{n-1}) 
$ 
is an isomorphism if $n\geqslant\max\{6,2q+1\}$. 
Thus, the cohomology of the family $\widetilde{\mathbf D}$ stabilizes.
<!-- end theorem-25 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The isomorphism~\eqref{FinDD} shows that, in order to prove the theorem, 
it is enough to establish the existence of canonical morphisms of complexes 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{K}_m}:\mathrm{K}_m(n)\longrightarrow \mathrm{K}_m(n-1), 
\qquad m\in\{1,2\}, 
\] 
which induce isomorphisms 
$ 
\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{K}_m}^*: 
H^q(\mathrm{K}_m(n))\longrightarrow H^q(\mathrm{K}_m(n-1)) 
$ 
if $n\geqslant 2q+1$. 
 
For $m=1$, use the canonical decompositions 
\eqref{K} and those established in the proofs of 
Lemmas~\ref{Dd0} and~\ref{HDDT0}: 
\[ 
\mathrm K_1(n)\cong 
\mathrm T_0(n-1)\oplus 
\mathrm T(n-1)^{\oplus2}\oplus 
\mathrm T^{(0)}_0(n-1)\oplus 
\mathrm T^{(2)}(n-1)^{\oplus2}. 
\] 
Define $\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm K_1}$ by the restrictions 
of $\mathrm{St}_D$ on $\mathrm T_0(n-1)$ and on both 
copies of $\mathrm T(n-1)$, and by zero on the 
remaining summands. 
This defines a morphism of complexes. 
 
For $n\geqslant\max\{6,2q+1\}$, 
Lemma~\ref{HTT}, the proof of Lemma~\ref{HDDT0}, 
and Corollary~\ref{A2} show that the additional 
summands have zero cohomology in degree $q$ 
in both the source and the target. 
On the remaining summands, the induced maps are 
isomorphisms by the proof of Theorem~\ref{StabS_D}. 
Hence $\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm K_1}^*$ is an 
isomorphism in degree $q$. 
 
Define the map $\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{K}_2}$ by 
\[ 
\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{K}_2}(x^l\times c\times y^r)= 
\begin{cases} 
x^l\times\mathrm{St}(c)\times y^r,&\text{if $l,r\geqslant 2$ and $l+r<n-1$},\\ 
0&\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\] 
Formula \eqref{BoundK2} shows that $\mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{K}_2}$ is a morphism of complexes. 
It induces a morphism of spectral sequences whose first pages are 
described by \eqref{SE1}. 
 
For $q\leqslant3$, both cohomology groups of $\mathrm K_2$ 
vanish. Let $q\geqslant4$ and 
$n\geqslant2q+1$. 
For $p\geqslant4$, $j\geqslant0$, and 
$p+j\in\{q-1,q,q+1\}$, we have 
\[ 
n-p-1\geqslant2j+p-2\geqslant2j+2. 
\] 
Thus Theorem~\ref{StabSH}, together with the elementary 
degree-zero case, shows that the induced map on $E_1$ 
is an isomorphism in these three total degrees. 
It follows that the map on $E_2$ is an isomorphism 
in total degree $q$. 
By Lemma~\ref{LmD2Zero}, both spectral sequences 
collapse at $E_2$. 
The induced map on the associated graded groups 
of $H^q$ is therefore an isomorphism. 
Since the filtrations are finite, the map on $H^q$ 
itself is an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- corr-15: body_md -->
\label{StableDD} 
For any $q\geqslant 2$ and $n\geqslant 2q+1$, 
the group $H^q\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf{D}}_n\bigr)$ stabilizes. 
The stable cohomology is given by the isomorphism: 
\begin{multline*} 
\qquad\qquad H^q(\widetilde{\mathbf D}_\infty) 
\cong 
H^q(\mathbf D_\infty) 
\oplus \\ 
\left[ 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant1} 
H^{q-2i-1}(\mathbf B_\infty)\otimes\mathbb Z_2 
\oplus 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant1} 
H^{q-2i}(\mathbf B_\infty)[2] 
\right] \\[1mm] 
\oplus 
\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{\substack{s\ {\rm even},\ s\geqslant4\\ j+s=q}} 
\bigl(\mathcal D^j_\infty\bigr)^{\oplus(s/2-1)}.\qquad\qquad 
\end{multline*} 
Thus, for any prime $p$, as well as for $p=0$, we have: 
\[ 
\mathrm{G}_p(\widetilde{\mathbf{D}}_\infty;t)= 
\begin{cases} 
\mathrm{G}_p(\mathbf{B}_\infty;t)&\text{if $p\neq 2$},\\[2mm] 
\mathrm{G}_2(\mathbf B_\infty;t)+\left(\frac{2t^2}{1-t}+\frac{t^4}{(1-t)^2}\right) 
\bigl(\mathrm{G}_2(\mathbf B_\infty;t)-1\bigr)&\text{if $p=2$}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-15 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{LmH}, the groups $\mathcal D^j_\infty$ are 
$2$-primary and satisfy 
\[ 
\sum_{j\geqslant0} 
\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\bigl(\mathcal D^j_\infty\otimes\mathbb F_2\bigr)t^j 
= 
(1+t)^2\bigl(\mathrm{G}_2(\mathbf B_\infty;t)-1\bigr). 
\] 
The stable decomposition follows from \eqref{FinDD}, Theorems~\ref{HK1} 
and~\ref{HK2}, Lemma~\ref{LmH}, and Corollary~\ref{StableD}. 
All summands outside $H^q(\mathbf D_\infty)$ are $2$-primary, so for 
$p\neq2$ they do not contribute to $\mathrm{G}_p$. This gives 
\[ 
\mathrm{G}_p(\widetilde{\mathbf D}_\infty;t)=\mathrm{G}_p(\mathbf B_\infty;t), 
\qquad p\neq2. 
\] 
For $p=2$, write $B(t)=\mathrm{G}_2(\mathbf B_\infty;t)$. By 
Corollary~\ref{StableD}, 
\[ 
\mathrm{G}_2(\mathbf{D}_\infty;t) 
= 
B(t)+\frac{t^2}{1-t}\bigl(B(t)-1\bigr). 
\] 
The second summand in the stable decomposition contributes another 
$\frac{t^2}{1-t}\bigl(B(t)-1\bigr)$. 
 
Since 
$\sum_{k\geqslant2}(k-1)t^{2k}=\frac{t^4}{(1-t^2)^2}$, 
the $K_2$-part contributes 
\[ 
(1+t)^2\bigl(B(t)-1\bigr) 
\sum_{k\geqslant2}(k-1)t^{2k}= 
\frac{t^4}{(1-t)^2}\bigl(B(t)-1\bigr). 
\] 
Adding these three contributions gives the stated formula.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corr-16: body_md -->
\label{HDQ} 
For $n\geqslant 5$, we have: 
\[ 
\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\;H^q\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf{D}}_n;\mathbb{Q}\bigr)= 
\begin{cases} 
1&\text{if $q=0, 1$},\\[1mm] 
\frac{n+3}{2}&\text{if $q=n-2$ and $n$ is odd},\\[1mm] 
\frac{n-2}{2}&\text{if $q=n-2$ and $n$ is even},\\[1mm] 
\frac{n+5}{2}&\text{if $q=n-1$ and $n$ is odd},\\[1mm] 
\frac{n}{2}&\text{if $q=n-1$ and $n$ is even},\\[1mm] 
0&\text{otherwise}. 
\end{cases} 
\]
<!-- end corr-16 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
According to the decomposition \eqref{FinDD}, we will evaluate the 
rational dimensions for both components in the non-trivial degrees $q=n-2$ and $q=n-1$. 
 
Step 1: \emph{Rational cohomology of $\mathrm{K}_1(n)$.} 
By Theorem \ref{HK1}, the rational cohomology of $\mathrm{K}_1(n)$ is assembled from 
$H^q(\mathbf{D}_{n-1};\mathbb{Q})$, the terms of the form $H^d(\mathrm{A}_2(m);\mathbb{Q})$,  
and the explicit top degree term $\mathbb{Z}^{\oplus 2}\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits\bigl[\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n)\mathbb{Z}\bigr]^{\oplus 2}$.  
From Corollary \ref{A2}, $H^d(\mathrm{A}_2(m);\mathbb{Q})$ is non-zero (and isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}$)  
if and only if $(m,d)=(0,0)$ or $(m,d)=(2,1)$. 
Evaluating these constraints: 
\begin{itemize} 
    \item[--] \textit{For $q=n-2$}:  
    If $n$ is odd, we collect $1$ from $H^{n-2}(\mathbf{D}_{n-1};\mathbb{Q})$. 
    The single sum  
    $$\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 1}H^{n-2-2i}(\mathrm{A}_2(n-2i-1))$$ contributes $\mathbb{Q}$  
    when $(m,d)=(2,1)$, meaning $n-2i-1=2$ and $n-2-2i=1$, which holds for $2i=n-3$. 
    The doubled sum $$\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{i\geqslant 2}H^{n-2-i}(\mathrm{A}_2(n-i-1))^{\oplus 2}$$ contributes $\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus 2}$  
    when $n-i-1=2$ and $n-2-i=1$, which holds for $i=n-3$. 
    Thus, for $n$ odd, $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}=1+1+2=4$.  
    If $n$ is even, both $\mathbf{D}_{n-1}$ and the single sum vanish (since $n-3$ is odd),  
    leaving only the doubled sum ($i=n-3$), which yields $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}=2$. 
    \item[--] \textit{For $q=n-1$}:  
    By Theorem \ref{HK1}, the rational dimension is entirely determined by the top degree term  
    $\mathbb{Z}^{\oplus 2} \oplus \bigl[\mathbb{Z}\big/\chi(n)\mathbb{Z}\bigr]^{\oplus 2} \otimes \mathbb{Q}$. 
    If $n$ is odd, $\chi(n)=0$, so the second term yields $\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus 2}$, giving a total $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}=2+2=4$.  
    If $n$ is even, $\chi(n)=2$, meaning the second term is pure torsion, leaving only the first term, so $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}=2$. 
\end{itemize} 
 
Step 2: \emph{Rational cohomology of $\mathrm{K}_2(n)$.} 
By Lemma~\ref{LmD2Zero}, the spectral sequence 
collapses at $E_2$. Hence the rational dimension of 
$H^q(\mathrm K_2(n))$ is the sum of the rational 
dimensions of the $E_2$-terms of total degree $q$. 
Tensoring with $\mathbb Q$ annihilates all torsion. 
By Lemma \ref{LmH}, the only non-zero rational groups are: 
\[ 
\left\{\mathrm{H}^{[0]}_0(0),\;\mathrm{H}^{[0]}_1(1),\; 
\mathrm{H}^{[1]}_0(2),\;\mathrm{H}^{[1]}_1(3)\right\}\otimes\mathbb{Q}\cong\left\{\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q}\right\}. 
\] 
Each corresponding block contributes exactly $1$ to the rational dimension, 
provided its assigned filtration $p=n-m-1$ is even (which enforces the parity of $n$), 
and the multiplicity is $\frac{p}{2}-1$. 
\begin{itemize} 
    \item[--] \textit{Degree $q=n-2$}:  
    If $n$ is odd, only the block containing $\mathrm{H}^{[1]}_0(2)$ 
    contributes ($p=n-3$), giving a dimension of $\frac{n-5}{2}$.  
    If $n$ is even, 
    the block containing $\mathrm{H}^{[1]}_1(3)$ ($p=n-4$) 
    gives $\frac{n-6}{2}$. 
    \item[--] \textit{Degree $q=n-1$}: 
  If $n$ is odd, only the block containing 
  $\mathrm H^{[0]}_0(0)$ contributes $(p=n-1)$, giving a dimension 
  of $\frac{n-3}{2}$. 
  If $n$ is even, only the block containing 
  $\mathrm H^{[0]}_1(1)$ contributes $(p=n-2)$, giving a dimension 
  of $\frac{n-4}{2}$. 
\end{itemize} 
 
Step 3: \emph{Total rational dimensions.} 
Adding the contributions from $\mathrm{K}_1(n)$ and $\mathrm{K}_2(n)$ yields the final rational ranks: 
\begin{itemize} 
    \item[--] \textit{For $q=n-2$}:  
    If $n$ is odd, $4+\frac{n-5}{2}=\frac{n+3}{2}$. If $n$ is even, $2+\frac{n-6}{2}=\frac{n-2}{2}$. 
    \item[--] \textit{For $q=n-1$}: 
    If $n$ is odd, $4+\frac{n-3}{2}=\frac{n+5}{2}$. If $n$ is even, $2+\frac{n-4}{2}=\frac{n}{2}$. 
\end{itemize} 
Apart from $H^0\cong H^1\cong\mathbb Q$, 
all remaining rational cohomology groups vanish.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- defnr-13: body_md -->
\label{Hcomp} 
The $k$--module 
\[ 
C_q(A;k):= 
\begin{cases} 
A_+^{\otimes q}&\text{if $q>0$},\\ 
k&\text{if $q=0$} 
\end{cases} 
\] 
is called the (normalized) \textit{module of chains of degree $q$ of the algebra $A$}. 
 
For $q>0$, elementary tensors we will write as 
$\bigl[a_1|\dots|a_q\bigr]$, where $a_i\in A_+$. 
If each $a_i$ is homogeneous, this is a \emph{homogeneous chain, of weight} 
\[ 
w\bigl[a_1|\dots|a_q\bigr]:=\sum_{i=1}^q w(a_i). 
\]
<!-- end defnr-13 -->
<!-- defnr-14: body_md -->
The sequence of homomorphisms 
\[ 
C_*(A;k):\quad k\stackrel{b}\longleftarrow C_1(A;k)\stackrel{b} 
\longleftarrow\cdots\stackrel{b}\longleftarrow C_{q-1}(A;k) 
\stackrel{b}\longleftarrow C_q(A;k)\stackrel{b}\longleftarrow\cdots, 
\] 
called the (Hochschild) \emph{differentials of $C_*(A;k)$}, is defined for $q>0$ by 
\[ 
b\bigl(\bigl[a_1|a_2|\dots|a_q\bigr]\bigr)= 
\sum_{i=1}^{q-1}(-1)^i\bigl[a_1|\dots|a_ia_{i+1}|\dots|a_q\bigr]. 
\] 
In particular, $b:C_1(A;k)\to C_0(A;k)=k$ is zero. 
 
This sequence forms a~complex, called the (normalized) 
\textit{Hochschild complex of the algebra $A$.} 
Its homology will be called the \emph{homology of the $k$-algebra $A$} 
(with trivial coefficients). 
\[ 
H_*(A;k):=\mathop{\mathbin{\scalebox{1}{$\bigoplus$}}}\nolimits_{q\geqslant 0}H_q(A;k), 
\] 
where $H_q(A;k)$ is the \emph{homology group in degree $q$}. 
For $h\in H_q(A;k)$, we write $\deg(h)=q$.
<!-- end defnr-14 -->
<!-- defnr-15: body_md -->
\label{Schuffle} 
For integers $q_1,q_2\geqslant 0$, a~permutation $\sigma\in S_{q_1+q_2}$ is a~\textit{$(q_1,q_2)$--shuffle} if 
\[ 
\sigma(1)<\sigma(2)<\dots<\sigma(q_1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad 
\sigma(q_1+1)<\sigma(q_1+2)<\dots<\sigma(q_1+q_2). 
\] 
The set of all $(q_1,q_2)$--shuffles is denoted by $Sh(q_1,q_2)$.
<!-- end defnr-15 -->
<!-- defnr-16: body_md -->
The operation $*$ by linearity defines a homomorphism of graded modules 
\[ 
C_*(A;k)\otimes C_*(B;k)\longrightarrow C_*(A\otimes B;k), 
\] 
called the \textit{shuffle product}.
<!-- end defnr-16 -->
<!-- theorem-26: body_md -->
\label{EZ}{\rm(\cite{MacL}, Ch.\Romannum{10},\S12.)} 
The operation $*$ satisfies the following identities: 
\begin{enumerate} 
  \item[\rm(a)] $b(x*y)=b(x)*y+(-1)^{\deg(x)}x*b(y)$, where $x\in C_{\deg(x)}(A;k),y\in C_*(B;k)$. 
\smallskip 
  \item[\rm(b)] If $x,y\in C_*(A;k)$, then, under the automorphism of 
$A\otimes A$ induced by the flip map 
\[ 
A\otimes A\longrightarrow A\otimes A,\qquad a\otimes b\mapsto b\otimes a, 
\] 
one has 
$x*y=(-1)^{\deg(x)\deg(y)}y*x$. 
  \smallskip 
  \item[\rm(c)] Under the canonical associativity identification of tensor 
products, one has 
\[ 
(x*y)*z=x*(y*z). 
\] 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-26 -->
<!-- defnr-17: body_md -->
\label{shprod} 
For algebras $A$ and $B$, consider the graded module homomorphism 
\[ 
\mathrm{EZ}:C_*(A;k)\otimes C_*(B;k)\to C_*(A\otimes B;k), 
\] 
defined by 
\[ 
\mathrm{EZ}\left( 
\bigl[a_1|\dots|a_{q_1}\bigr]\otimes\bigl[b_1|\dots|b_{q_2}\bigr] 
\right) 
:= 
\bigl[a_1|\dots|a_{q_1}\bigr]*\bigl[b_1|\dots|b_{q_2}\bigr]. 
\] 
This map is called the \textit{Eilenberg--Zilber homomorphism}.
<!-- end defnr-17 -->
<!-- theorem-27: body_md -->
\label{ttth1} 
The homomorphism $\mathrm{EZ}$ is a morphism of complexes. 
If both $A$ and $H_*(A;k)$ are free $k$--modules, 
then, for every $B\in\mathcal A$, the K\"unneth identification 
\[ 
H_*\bigl(C_*(A;k)\otimes C_*(B;k)\bigr) 
\cong H_*(A;k)\otimes H_*(B;k) 
\] 
gives an induced isomorphism 
\[ 
\mathrm{EZ}_*:H_*(A;k)\otimes H_*(B;k)\longrightarrow H_*(A\otimes B;k). 
\]
<!-- end theorem-27 -->
<!-- corr-17: body_md -->
\label{ttth2} 
For $A\in\mathcal A$, the composition 
\[ 
H_*(A;k)\otimes H_*(A;k)\stackrel{\mathrm{EZ}_*}{\longrightarrow} 
H_*(A\otimes A;k)\stackrel{\mu_*}{\longrightarrow} H_*(A;k) 
\] 
endows $H_*(A;k)$ with the structure of a graded-commutative algebra.
<!-- end corr-17 -->
<!-- defnr-18: body_md -->
\label{dPon} 
The graded-commutative algebra structure on $H_*(A;k)$ defined in 
Corollary~\ref{ttth2} is called the \emph{Pontryagin algebra of $A$}.
<!-- end defnr-18 -->
<!-- defnr-19: body_md -->
\label{AW} 
For algebras $A$ and $B$, consider the graded module homomorphism 
\[ 
\mathrm{AW}:C_*(A\otimes B;k)\longrightarrow C_*(A;k)\otimes C_*(B;k), 
\] 
defined by 
\[ 
\mathrm{AW}\bigl[a_1\otimes b_1|\cdots|a_q\otimes b_q\bigr] 
:=\sum_{r=0}^{q} 
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{r}\varepsilon_B(b_i)\right) 
\left(\prod_{i=r+1}^{q}\varepsilon_A(a_i)\right) 
\bigl[\bar a_1|\cdots|\bar a_r\bigr]\otimes 
\bigl[\bar b_{r+1}|\cdots|\bar b_q\bigr]. 
\] 
This map is called the \emph{Alexander–Whitney homomorphism}.
<!-- end defnr-19 -->
<!-- theorem-28: body_md -->
\label{AWH} 
The homomorphism $\mathrm{AW}$ is a~morphism of complexes. 
If both $A$ and $H_*(A;k)$ are free $k$--modules, then for any algebra $B$ the induced map 
\[ 
\mathrm{AW}_*:H_*(A\otimes B;k)\longrightarrow H_*(A;k)\otimes H_*(B;k) 
\] 
is an isomorphism of $k$--modules, inverse to the isomorphism $\mathrm{EZ}_*$.
<!-- end theorem-28 -->
